1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Overview
This Program Review provides a stocktaking of USAID's information integrity and resilience
(IIR) activities around the world. It comes at a critical time for the agency and development
partners. On the one hand, there is a growing sense that mis-, dis-, and mal-information (MDM)
pose serious threats to democratic institutions, health interventions, and broad foreign policy
objectives related to peace and stability. In response, USAID and other partners have expanded
support toprojects that aim to increase the supply of high quality information from independent,
credible sources and build societal resilience to MDM from malign actors, including anti-
democratic leaders and foreign governments. This work cuts across multiple sectors and offices
at USAID, including Democracy, Human Rights, and Governance (DRG), Health, the Office of
Transitional Initiatives (OTI), and others. While USAID has supported programming in this space
for decades, the focus on countering MDM is relatively new. By some accounts, it began in the
late 2000s and is reflected in program objectives only in the last five years.
At the same time, important ongoing debates raise questions about the appropriate scale and
scope of USAID's support for IIR interventions. There is concern that efforts to counter foreign
malign influence might distract from more pressing development goals, especially those
addressed by long-standing media development efforts.! Relatedly, some question whether IIR
strategies—particularly efforts to counter misinformation spread by malign actors-can be
effective both overall and in the most difficult contexts. While decades of research and
experience provide an evidence base for interventions related to media development, less is
known about strategies that aim to build societal resilience to non-credible information and
counter MDM. Another question is whether USAID should be engaged in social and behavior
change initiatives that seek to influence specific attitudes and beliefs. While such approaches

GS-10F-0033M / 7200AA18M00016, Tasking N088
Nicaragua, Tanzania, and Libya. In the case study countries, the research team conducted in-
depth research through key informant interviews (Klls) with Mission and IP staff, in addition to
reviewing program documents. While no set of cases can fully capture the depth and breadth of
USAID's IIR programming, the cases were selected in coordination with USAID to be
representative of the main contexts where USAID implements IR activities and the types of
interventions it supports.
The report's findings and recommendations are based on two information sources: an extensive
document review of more than 200 program documents provided by USAID and IPs, and 20
Klls with 41 individuals, including USAID and IP personnel based in t the United States and
overseas.4
The projects included in this review operate in very different contexts and address distinct
issues and harms. Many projects are implemented in new and emerging democracies, where an
urgent priority is to support the emergence and capacity of independent media actors. Others
are implemented in countries where governments are hostile to media freedom or spread mis-
and dis-information for instrumental political reasons. Another set of projects operate in contexts
where malign foreign actors use MDM to weaken democratic institutions and undermine support
for the West and aligned governments.
USAID's IIR programming encompasses a wide set of activities. Several included in this review
focus on media development, building on USAID's long-standing efforts to foster independent,
high-quality media around the world by training journalists, improving newsroom capacity, and
improving the economic and regulatory environment for media. Typically, media development
activities do not conceptualize their goals in terms of countering MDM; more often, they aim to
improve the overall information ecosystem, contributing indirectly, if at all, to MDM efforts.
Examples include the Media Program in Ukraine (MPU), Strengthening Media Systems in
Serbia, and the Media Sector Development Activity in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Other activities—such as the Tanzania Media and Civil Society Strengthening (TMCS) Activity,
the Media Strengthening Program in Nicaragua, the Assisting Independent New Supply project
in Venezuela, and the Cultivating Media Independence project in the Kyrgyz Republic (MEDIA-
K) —provide critical lifelines to media outlets facing regimes that are hostile to independent
information sources.
Multiple projects covered by this review focus on building societal resilience through media
literacy and public education. For example, the Media Literacy Program in Indonesia uses a set
of innovative strategies to inculcate skills needed to distinguish credible information sources
from MDM, particularly among new digital arrivals. In North Macedonia, USAID activities work
with the national education system to provide media literacy training through schools. In Latin
America, a regional activity helps in-country steering committees design civil society projects to
promote media literacy among young people.
4 The research team was not able to arrange interviews for one of the selected case study countries,
Tanzania.

GS-10F-0033M / 7200AA18M00016, Tasking N088
A smaller number of activities in the review include components that directly aim to counter
MDM through strategies including fact-checking, debunking, trust and safety strengthening, and
strategic narratives. In Ukraine, USAID's flagship IIR program, activities include a wide range of
interventions, including components designed to counter false narratives from Russian news
and social media related to the on-going war in Ukraine. One project, Breakthrough ACTION,
focuses on combatting misinformation in the health sector, while two others aim to support civil
society through regional hubs that build and support multi-country networks.
To conceptualize the current scope of USAID's investments in IIR programming as represented
by the 23 projects included in this review, the research team developed an updated typology
(see Figure 1 in Section 4) based on an initial version created by USAID's Democracy,
Resilience, and Innovation (DRI) Team. The typology groups activities into five broad categories
with distinct goals and approaches. It relates these categories to the "supply and demand"
conceptualization commonly used in IIR programming and shows how they overlap with goals
related to Information Resilience (the ability of news ecosystems to produce high-quality,
trustworthy content and citizens to access, identify, and interpret that content) and Harm
Mitigation & Integrity (responses to the dissemination of MDM and the harms attributed to it),
building on newer conceptualization of the IIR space.
The expanding focus on information integrity and resilience within USAID has created a need to
take stock of current MERL approaches and to develop strategies for expanding the evidence
base where gaps exist. Due to the inherent challenges of studying the effects of IIR activities on
higher-order outcomes, donors and IPs typically focus on tracking outputs and short-term
outcomes. Despite this, the document review and Klls with USAID staff and IPs found a
substantial evidence base for some interventions, particularly related to media development and
media literacy/public education. While the evidence base for some newer approaches,
particularly those that aim to directly counter MDM, is less developed, the review did not find
evidence that any current approaches should be curtailed. As outlined below, the review
recommends greater investment in MERL efforts to build the evidence base in several areas
using a combination of qualitative and quantitative approaches.
Key Findings
The review offers 12 key findings, developed more fully in the main body of the report. An
important caveat is that the findings are based on the 23 projects included in this review, not the
full universe of USAID activities that relate to IIR goals. Accordingly, the findings are not
exhaustive and may not be applicable to activity types not covered by this review. The findings
are ordered sequentially according to the structure of the report, with those related to the
stocktaking of activities first and others that relate to cross-cutting issues, MERL approaches,
and program effectiveness following. This ordering is not meant to convey the relative
importance of the individual findings.
1. Among the 23 activities reviewed, programming is concentrated in two main areas:
media development and media literacy/public education. A smaller set of activities focus
on supporting civil society; monitoring, understanding, and directly countering MDM; and
USAID.GOV
PROGRAM REVIEW OF USAID INFORMATION INTEGRITY AND RESILIENCE ACTIVITIES
]10

GS-10F-0033M / 7200AA18M00016, Tasking N088
responding to MDM through strategic communications offering alternative narratives or
debunking disinformation narratives.
2. While some activities explicitly seek to counter malign foreign influence, most
reviewed for this report do not. Instead, many activities focus on other harms like limited
government accountability, behaviors that negatively impact public health or social stability,
and broader harms to democracy.
3. The diversity of USAID's IIR activities poses challenges for developing consistent
approaches, TOCs, MERL strategies, and cumulative learnings. USAID currently
supports a wide range of activities that respond to distinct issues in very different contexts.
The objectives, TOCs, and MERL strategies reflect the diversity of activities, goals, and
settings—making it difficult to develop standardized approaches and to accumulate
evidence on what works in USAID's IIR programming. While the available data is rich, it is
more useful for answering questions about impact on the media sector or uptake of training
materials than prevention or manipulation via MDM. Few activities are set up directly to
address MDM and measure their effectiveness against that goal—a reflection of how new
this priority is for USAID and the inherent challenges of measuring effects in the absence of
counterfactuals.
4. Within USAID, there are differing views about the goals and objectives of IIR
activities. USAID staff consulted for this report noted some important distinctions in how
they understand core objectives. Some respondents conceptualize interventions as
promoting information integrity and building a resilient media environment by ensuring the
availability of credible information sources, while others view their efforts as designed to
directly counter MDM, often related to context-specific threats and actors. While these
differences may in part reflect contextual differences or lack of agreement on shared
terminology, they have deeper significance since alternative frames inform how program
designers and implementers conceive the theory of change and articulate the associated
harms they aim to mitigate.
5. Respondents disagree on whether IIR activities should aim to produce social and
behavior change. Even within the same program, IPs and USAID staff sometimes
disagreed on whether behavior and attitudinal change was the goal of an activity or an
appropriate measure of its success. This was especially true for media development and
media literacy activities. However, in public health activities and strategic communications
(specifically the Georgia Information Integrity Project), activities are explicitly aimed at
changing individual attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors. Some USAID staff questioned whether
strategic communications is part of USAID's remit, while others cheered these approaches
as innovative and more directly responsive to MDM than more common media development
activities.
6. Relatedly, views differed on whether USAID is the right actor to pursue some types of
strategic communications programming. The program review included two examples of
activities categorized as strategic communications. USAID staff expressed uncertainty about

whether this approach should be adapted more widely across the Agency. Some expressed
concern that it is more suited to State Department public diplomacy efforts than international
development activities.
7. While there is widespread support for addressing cross-cutting issues related to
gender and marginalized/vulnerable groups, few activities make this a central goal.
Respondents expressed support for the general idea that USAID and IPs should do more to
address MDM related to gender and marginalized groups, including online harassment that
may increase the risks of violence against these groups and discourage participation in
politics, among other harms. Respondents agreed that these issues were often not
adequately considered during program design. Consistent with this, the program review
found that only eight of 23 activities incorporated cross-cutting issues in meaningful ways.
8. Respondents held differing views on whether IIR activities should be targeted to
address harms related to specific population segments. Some interviewees expressed
support for IIR activities designed to address group-specific harms experienced by women
and marginalized/vulnerable groups. However, others viewed activities as taking a "whole-
of-society" approach that benefited all social segments, making targeting unnecessary.
Additionally, there did not appear to be any programs addressing MDM with an
understanding of how gender norms and social cleavages are manipulated through
disinformation campaigns in order to influence political outcomes, including elections and
policy decisions. Some programs responded to instances of online violence against women
but they did not appear to be central objectives of any under this revieweven though
gendered disinformation and misogynist narratives are a key strategy of some authoritarian
governments.
9. TOCs are typically not assessed by existing MERL approaches. The TOCs articulated
in project documents often emphasize high-level, long-term impacts, including increased
availability of quality information, greater demand for impartial information, increased citizen
participation, improved inclusion and tolerance, and greater transparency and accountability
in government. These objectives are often long-term goals that would require decades to
achieve, even under the most favorable conditions. MERL plans, on the other hand, tend to
focus on outputs and short-term outcomes, including the number of journalists trained and
workshops held, the number of legal reforms attempted, the reach of content produced by
USAID-supported actors, and other related measures.
10. The focus on outputs and short-term outcomes in MERL plans reflects the inherent
difficulties of measuring long-term outcomes and impacts for most IIR activities. IIR
activities often face daunting challenges in assessing effectiveness since counterfactuals
cannot be observed, limiting opportunities to measure higher-order impacts with common
M&E indicators and approaches. In addition, many programs included in this review have

not existed for long enough to measure their long-term impacts. Moreover, in some cases it
is neither desirable nor feasible to focus on impacts, including in conflict-affected and
transitioning countries, where evolving political conditions and project objectives may limit
opportunities for measuring impacts. In other cases, though, opportunities exist for
integrating MERL approaches that have the potential to narrow the gap between the goals
expressed in TOCs and the data collected to track program effects.
11. There is a substantial evidence base for some well-established IIR interventions,
particularly in relation to intermediate objectives. M&E data and academic literature
suggest that media development and media literacy activities can be effective at building the
capacity of media organizations and other stakeholders to provide accurate, unbiased
information and helping citizens navigate complex information landscapes. However,
because many media development projects were designed before countering MDM became
a USAID priority, indicators and MERL plans for these activities seldom assess their broader
impact on MDM.
12. The evidence base for some approaches, particularly newer, innovative strategies for
countering MDM, is more limited. Some activities included in this review were too early in
their implementation to provide concrete evidence of effectiveness. For example, Ecuador
Verifica has just completed its first year. In addition, for some activity types it is not possible
to assess the extent of the evidence base since only a small number or relevant activities
were included in this review. For example, only two activities out of 23 focused on strategic
communications. While the report offers insights from those activities, the research team
cannot make broad inferences about the effectiveness of the overall approach from such a
small sample.
Summary of Recommendations
Based on the key findings outlined above, as well as others described in subsequent sections,
we offer a set of recommendations related to programming and MERL approaches to USAID
and its partners. The recommendations are outlined in more detail at the end of the report. The
ordering is not meant to reflect prioritization of some recommendations over others.
Programmatic Recommendations
1. Make long-term investments in information integrity and resilience while pursuing
short-term harm mitigation. USAID must be able to pursue both long-term change and
rapid responses to emerging threats simultaneously. Whether short- or long-term
approaches are most appropriate will depend on specific program objectives and contexts.
For example, during elections, on-going conflicts, or crisis situations, a generational program
to improve government accountability is not responsive to pressing needs. In these
situations, USAID should have a ready set of short-term approaches to mitigate the risk of
serious harms. More generally, however, USAID should invest in longer-term efforts to
strengthen media environments and improve how citizens navigate information landscapes,
building resilience to future shocks and challenges. Some activities, including strategio
USAID.GOV

113

GS-10F-0033M / 7200AA18M00016, Tasking N088
communications capacity building, can address both short- and long-term objectives at the
same time: by enhancing civil society's ability to influence public discourse through values-
based messaging, USAID activities can promote long-term infrastructure used for advocacy
of democratic values while also addressing more immediate threats.
2. Continue pursuing media development objectives independent of the IIR agenda-but
where appropriate, tie those activities to IIR-related goals and indicators and study
the relationship between the two areas more closely. Media development activities have
demonstrated positive effects on indicators related to their longstanding objectives: they can
quantify, for example, increases in revenue after adoption of best practices or improvements
in the perceived credibility of news content. However, as noted in the previous
recommendation, they do not typically measure whether investments in independent media
produce follow-on benefits by counteracting harms from MDM related to civic participation,
social cohesion, or societal distrust. A robust independent media is necessary but not
sufficient for information resilience. If USAID activities want media development activities to
speak more directly to harms from MDM, they should adopt directly relevant MERL
approaches. Additionally, USAID could support internal and external research exploring the
relationship between media development and information resilience more closely.
3. Prioritize testing and refining media literacy approaches. Media literacy and public
education are common components of IIR activities. As described in Section 4, the review
found that 43 percent (10 of 23) of activities included such components. Both USAID MERL
data and academic literature suggest that media literacy can be effective at reducing the
audience and impact of low-integrity information. However, few USAID activities are set up
to assess whether the provision of media literacy education leads to enduring changes in
behavior such as verifying source credibility or avoiding untrustworthy outlets. An exception
is the Advancing Media Literacy project in Indonesia, which iteratively tests and improves
digital media literacy campaign strategies and publishes the results in scholarly journals.
The content of curricula also varies widely. Academic literature provides many competing
variants of "media literacy" and suggests that information literacy specifically is important for
resilience against MDM. Given the prominence and promise of this intervention type, greater
resources should be devoted to studying the effectiveness of differing media literacy
approaches, curricula, and delivery mechanisms, with programmatic refinements made
based on the evolving evidence base.
4. Consider whether and how to proceed with strategic communications activities
designed to counter MDM in the political sphere. Despite the promise of strategic
communications activities, few activities included in this review adopt this strategy. USAID
should pause to consider whether and how it wants to proceed in this area of programming,
which carries both promise and risk. In doing so, it should emphasize collecting more
evidence of impact. As noted, the limited number of activities of this type included in this
review makes it difficult to adequately assess this approach.
USAID.GOV

GS-10F-0033M / 7200AA18M00016, Tasking N088
5. Fund iterative, experimental activities designed to generate insights for future
activities. USAID should support activities designed to test and repeat common approaches
to fill crucial knowledge gaps. These might be shorter term initiatives or longer activities
designed to include multiple iterative cycles. For example, USAID could explore the most
effective ways to deliver media literacy training to adults outside the classroom through an
iterative, adaptive program in one or more countries—borrowing insights from the Advancing
Media Literacy project in Indonesia.
6. Consider ways of integrating non-media programming more fully in the information
resilience and counter-MDM toolkit. As noted above, media development is the most
common IIR activity type included in the activities covered by this report. In interviews,
USAID staff and partners frequently mentioned activities using the arts and other avenues to
promote social dialogue around key issues, like the public "Propagandarium" virtual reality
exhibit on media literacy in [contact omitted] partnerships with folk musicians in Georgia. USAID
should expand linkages between media and other activities to avoid missing valuable
opportunities to address IIR issues more holistically.
7. Develop objectives that match project scopes and timelines. For activities with TOCs,
this means making them more narrow, achievable, and measurable by including a series of
more modest, discrete steps that can be completed in the allotted timeframe and with
available resources. Activities without a formal theory of change should also develop
specific, achievable, and attributable objectives that reflect project timelines and the scope
of activities. While this recommendation relates to MERL approaches, it is also important at
the program design stage.

2. INTRODUCTION
As part of the Democracy, Human Rights, and Governance Learning, Evaluation, and Research
(DRG-LER) I| Activity, USAID asked NORC at the University of Chicago to carry out a program
review of USAID's information integrity and resilience programming. This review aims to inform
USAID's Democracy, Resilience, and Innovation Team's efforts to identify promising
approaches, develop tools and trainings for USAID staff and to inform potential program design
and USAID activities. This study will also help improve USAID's MERL strategies.
Goals and Research Questions
The goal of the program review is to examine a representative set of USAID-funded activities
related to information integrity and resilience. This review does not serve as an evaluation of
USAID-funded activities; rather, it aims to take stock of USAID programming and examine
TOCs, approaches to cross-cutting issues, monitoring and evaluation strategies, and evidence
of effectiveness. The review is guided by a set of research questions (RQs) initially presented in
the Concept Note for this task and subsequently refined with input from USAID after project
launch:
(RQ1) Theories of Change. How do USAID projects define information integrity and
resilience and conceptualize the harms associated with MDM? What types of theories of
change are being used by projects seeking to prevent or address these harms? Are there
ways to improve TOCs for USAID's activities?
(RQ2) Stocktaking of Activities. What approaches are USAID and its implementing
partners using to build information integrity and resilience and to counter MDM? How are
these related to the above theories of change? What is the appropriate typology for
information integrity and resilience projects and adjacent activities? Are there types of
activities that are over-or under-represented?
(RQ3) Stocktaking of Approaches Related to Cross-Cutting Issues. What share of
projects are addressing issues related to gender and marginalized groups (e.g., immigrants,
minorities, LGBTQI+ communities, etc.)? What strategies are being used?

Methodology
Document review. The research team compiled and examined more than 200 program
documents provided by USAID related to 23 activities. The set of 23 activities was chosen by
USAID from a list of more than 70 projects to provide a representative sample of the types of IIR
activities supported by USAID and the contexts in which they are implemented.? Documents
included: (1) program work plans, (2) quarterly and annual reports, (3) MERL plans, and (4)
evaluation/research reports (see Annex G for a complete list of documents). Based on this
material, the team catalogued activities by type, refined the typology of USAID information
integrity and resilience programming, and analyzed information related to the core research
questions, focusing on TOCs, MERL strategies, cross-cutting issues, and evidence of impact.
Key Informant Interviews. The study team conducted 23 Klls with a total of 45 participants.
This included interviews with headquarters personnel from USAID and Implementing Partners.
The team also conducted interviews with USAID Mission staff and IPs in six case study
countries: Ukraine, Georgia, Serbia, Libya, Nicaragua, and Indonesia.® The Klls for the case
studies were designed to complement information obtained through the document review and
allow for further exploration of core topics. The set of case study countries was chosen in
collaboration with USAID to ensure the inclusion of multiple project types and implementing
partners, and to cover multiple regions and political regime types. The study team conducted all
Klls remotely between May 12 and July 14, 2023.

3. STOCKTAKING OF THEORIES OF CHANGE
RQ1.1: How do USAID activities define information integrity and resilience and
conceptualize the harms associated with MDM?
RQ1.2: What types of TOCs are being used by activities seeking to prevent or address
these harms?
This section explores competing conceptions of the core problem, examines the types of harms
activities aim to address, and summarizes common interventions used to prevent or mitigate
those harms. It also discusses how activities describe what they aim to achieve and how they
hope to achieve it—often referred to as a "theory of change."
The distinction between promoting high-integrity information and a resilient media environment
and countering or preventing harms from MDM was an important theme during interviews.
Which of these frames an activity used often informs its TOC—as does the way it articulates the
associated harms.
Among the 23 activities included in this review, 12 contained an explicit TOC in documents
provided to the research team (see Annex B). For activities without an explicit TOC, the
research team inferred an implied TOC from stated objectives. The team also inquired about
TOCs during Klls for the case study countries. Kll participants conveyed that the TOC pursued
by an activity is influenced by multiple factors, including the social and political context, the
overall donor landscape in a country, and the available implementing partners. While
responding to malign foreign influence is often a goal of IIR activities, many focused on other
harms such as reduced government accountability, behaviors that negatively impact public
health or social stability, or abstract harms to democracy. The most sophisticated TOCs
associated low-integrity information with specific harms and identified appropriate interventions.

Definitional questions limit most attempts to describe the harms associated with mis-, dis-, and
mal-information. All Kll participants were familiar with the term MDM as laid out by Wardle and
Hossein's work on "Information Disorder." Respondents typically understood these terms as
Wardle and Hossein do: misinformation is the incidental, unintentional spread of false or
misleading information-essentially rumors—while disinformation is understood to be
intentional. (Mal-information is used less commonly and refers to accurate information used
intentionally to harm, such as the release of hacked materials.) Some interview participants felt
these terms and definitions, while widely cited, lacked a necessary degree of clarity around
nuanced and sometimes sensitive issues. Several expressed an appetite for more precise
terms, noting for example that even "MDM" obscures important differences between mis- and
disinformation. Others said that terms like "countering MDM" and "foreign interference" evoke
geopolitical aspects of strategic communications by external authoritarian governments,
sometimes in contexts where domestic sources of MDM were more influential and harmful.
Interviewees also expressed concern that responding to foreign influence does little to address
underlying social issues such as food insecurity or conflict—which mis- and disinformation can
exacerbate but rarely cause.
Wardle and Hossein's "MDM" construct is not the only definition on offer. While this report does
not endorse one framework in what remains an on-going debate, alternatives can provide useful
insights. The National Science and Technology Council, a U.S. government (USG) interagency
working group, provided a useful alternative in a December 2022 "Roadmap for Researchers on
Priorities Related to Information Integrity Research and Development." It distinguished between
"high-integrity" and "low integrity information" and defined "resilience" as the ability of people to
operate in the context of potentially questionable information and of communities to "maintain
appropriate levels of information integrity" despite uncertainty or active manipulations."'' It
described this as a separate priority from preventing or minimizing "avoidable harms" from
information manipulation (a term with significant overlap with the "disinformation" component of
"MDM").

4. STOCKTAKING OF ACTIVITIES
RQ2.1: What approaches are USAID and its implementing partners using to build
information integrity and resilience and to counter MDM?

RQ2.3: What is the appropriate typology for information integrity and resilience activities

This section takes stock of USAID's information resilience and integrity activities, identifying
common approaches, relating activities to theories of change, and noting gaps in programming.
It also provides an updated typology of USAID-funded activities designed to assist USAID in
communicating current IIR programming in a concise, visual format for a variety of audiences,
including Mission personnel and others interested in exploring potential intervention strategies.
Across this new typology, the most prominent activities are those related to media development
and support, followed by media literacy efforts. These types of activities promote "information
resilience," though media literacy can also be considered a form of harm mitigation. Less well-
represented are "counter-MDM" approaches that aim to understand and respond directly to low-
integrity information and its purveyors. Several include research and media monitoring
components; only a few incorporate strategic communications or "information resilience hubs"
designed to promote collaboration.
A Proposed Typology for USAID Activities Included in This Review
The proposed typology in Figure 1 aims offers a simple framework that groups current USAID
IIR activities—as represented by the 23 activities included in this review—into a smaller number
of broad categories. These are the same categories developed for the TOCs above; they apply
as well to the assumptions and objectives behind activities as they do to the activities
themselves. They are not meant to be reflective of the totality of U.S. government programming
in this space. Other institutions, like the State Department and the Department of Defense, have
their own activities, some of which overlap with this typology but some of which may not.
Activities implemented by other government agencies are beyond the scope of this review.
As a starting point, the research team considered the initial typology developed by USAID
(included in Annex F). This typology captured most of the activities included in this review, but
its nine categories had significant overlap. For example, legal and regulatory reform was
included both as its own category and as an activity under media development. To make the

The original typology also offered little analysis about how different categories addressed
information resilience and MDM and how they compared with one another. This typology
attempts to address this by organizing activities across two axes. First, column labels on the top
of the typology show how the five categories relate to core goals connected to (1) information
resilience (activities improving media production and consumption) and (2) harm mitigation and
information integrity (activities focused more directly on understanding and reducing the effects
of low-integrity information). Second, labels on the left show how the categories relate to the
supply-demand categorization scheme that is commonly used to describe IIR/MDM approaches.
Information resilience hubs, in the middle, increase capacity across other categories.
Two additional points are important. First, many USAID-funded IIR program contain multiple
activities, with components in more than one category. It is probably not feasible—or even
helpful—to create a typology in which each program fits into only one category. Second, an
important caveat is that the revised typology is based on the 23 activities included in this review
and does not reflect other activity types that USAID—or other donors and IPs—may support.

Media literacy activities are both conceptually and practically diverse: there are many definitions
of media literacy and many ways to deliver training. In Indonesia, USAID has partnered with a
university to assess the effectiveness of an online game, memes, and short form videos at
delivering media literacy education to populations known to engage MDM. In Ukraine, the MPU
also contains a large media literacy component: it offers training to teachers, librarians, and
other professionals as well as novel sources of media literacy awareness such as public
exhibitions. In Ukraine these trainings teach media consumers to recognize, check, and avoid
untrustworthy sources of information. Meanwhile, in Serbia, USAID's MIPS program teaches
news consumers about the country's media landscape, how media ownership is distributed, and
how journalism is produced in Serbian society.
TOCs in this category often emphasize the relationship between a robust media and an
informed citizenry capable of holding government actors accountable—what one program called
a "vibrant, independent media sector capable of shaping democratic discourse." They
sometimes frame this as increasing "demand" for high-quality content by helping citizens
recognize and access trustworthy journalism. The relationship between supply and demand
means there is significant overlap between Category | (systemic and operational support for
media) and Category II (improving citizen engagement with media). Most projects with activities
in Category Il also included components in Category I.
Category III: Understanding, Exposing, and Responding to MDM (8 of 23 activities). This
category includes efforts to monitor disinformation, expose its sources, understand how it
spreads, and evaluate or pursue appropriate responses. Sometimes this takes the form of

addition to correcting claims for the public, it can also fit in this category. Likewise, efforts to
strengthen social media platform trust and safety fit in this category. Because these activities
take MDM and its spread as their focus, they are considered to be "supply-side" activities
looking to detect and reduce low-integrity information.

Across the 23 activities included in this review, there was significant variation in the extent to
which activities prioritized and addressed cross-cutting issues, including GESI and engagement
of marginalized groups (e.g., youth, immigrants, minorities, indigenous, disabled, and LGBTQI+
communities.). Of the 23 activities reviewed, eight incorporated these cross-cutting issues in
meaningfult ways and nine did so in cursory1 ways. For the other six, the research team found
no evidence of GESI inclusion in the documents we reviewed and the discussions we had with
program staff. However, it should be noted that the research team only had interviews with
personnel involved in two of the six activities that had not incorporated GESI principles, and it is
possible that we were simply missing GESI-related documents for the others.

TOCs. A key finding is that most MEL plans focus on output and short-term outcomes rather
than higher-order impacts. While this reflects the inherent difficulty of measuring impacts for
most IIR activities, it means that TOCs often cannot be assessed with project M&E data. Finally,
the section notes that Kll respondents consistently reported MERL efforts are hampered by
insufficient resources, including funds, time, and staff availability.
M&E Strategies
The MERL strategies used by activities can be categorized into two types of approaches:
theory-based [contact omitted] CAMEL." These are complementary approaches that are often used
together. All activities in this review engaged in theory-based MERL by developing results
frameworks and collecting monitoring data on preselected indicators.1 Complexity-aware
approaches are used by some activities to track unpredicted outcomes.
Theory-based MERL is the more common approach. It focuses on assessing the predictable
aspects of an activity based on work plans, results frameworks, and TOCs. This type of MERL
typically uses indicators and targets to assess an activity's progress. Complexity-aware
approaches, on the other hand, focus on monitoring unpredictable aspects of an activity. This
includes identifying changes in the external context of the program, emergent or unexpected
program outcomes, and other uncertain or contested aspects of an activity. The complexity-
aware approach typically does not use indicators or targets, which would require predictions.
Instead, activities identify aspects of the program that may be vulnerable to complexity by noting
the outcomes that might be at risk if key assumptions do not hold or areas where outcomes are
simply difficult to predict in advance. Then, the program collects data on those areas so it can
adapt, as needed.
Review of Indicators
The vast majority of indicators included in M&E plans measure program outputs (e.g., number of
people reached, number of social media acts of engagement) or short-term outcomes (e.g.,
percent of trainees with increased knowledge after the training, average increase in revenue for
supported media organizations). Few indicators of longer-term outcomes or impact were noted.

Interview respondents noted several challenges in measuring the outcomes and impact of IIR
and countering MDM activities. Chief among these challenges is the fact that IIR/MDM take
place in complex, ever-changing contexts and we have very limited knowledge about how
changes in the context affect activity goals. Thus, it is difficult to assess the degree to which
observed outcomes and impacts can be attributed to the activity.
Interview respondents noted that building IIR and countering MDM are "complex" or "wicked"
problems - posing significant challenges for developing appropriate MERL strategies. Complex
problems are those for which there are key knowledge gaps in the scientific evidence about the
problem or the solutions, and for which multiple stakeholders, each with different expertise and
knowledge gaps, are required to address the issue. Evidence-based decisions are often difficult
to make because of gaps in knowledge. Wicked problems are those for which there is minimal
scientific evidence about the problem or the solutions, and multiple stakeholders, often with
conflicting values or interests, are required to address the issue. Making purely evidence-based
decisions is often impossible, due not only to the lack of evidence but also to the lack of
agreement among stakeholders. 19,20
Because of this complexity or wickedness, and because addressing IIR/MDM issues typically
requires changes to entire systems (e.g., media environments, social attitudes or cohesion), it
can be difficult or impossible to predict all the effects an activity will have on society. Many
activities acknowledged this and integrated complexity-aware MEL approaches into their MEL
plans to monitor for emergent activity outcomes or changes in context that would affect the
activity's ability to meet their intended outcomes. CAMEL approaches used in the activities we
reviewed include outcome harvesting; the use of sentinel indicators to watch for changes in
context; developing and implementing learning agendas that cover complex aspects of an
activity, like how to build audience trust; and conducting learning activities, such as pause and
reflect sessions.
The other major challenge reported was a lack of appropriate resources for MEL. Respondents
were quick to point out that the resources needed include funding, time, and staff. It can be
difficult to find MEL experts with sufficient complexity-aware and systems-thinking skills to
support IIR/MDM activities. Furthermore, to do complexity-aware monitoring well, activities
either need more time or they need to reduce the size of their theory-based monitoring plans so
staff can shift their focus. Respondents also noted that it would be helpful for USAID to provide
more encouragement to update TOCs and results frameworks as activities adapt to changes in
the context or in USAID requirements.

7. ANALYSIS OF IMPACT
RQ5.1: Which current approaches seem to be working best to increase information
resilience and integrity and to address MDM?
RQ5.2: Which current approaches have the most evidence to support their
effectiveness?
RQ5.3: What contextual factors affect the impact of these approaches?
This section presents key findings related to the analysis of what's working, the evidence base
for assessing effectiveness, and contextual factors. The findings reflect perspectives shared
with the research team by USAID personnel and IPs, along with the team's own review of the
available evidence from M&E documents, evaluations, and other activity materials. We outline
three principal findings organized in relation to the five categories of activities defined by the
proposed typology in Section 4.
First, there is a substantial evidence base for activities in Category 1: Media
Organizational and Systemic Support. Evidence shows these activities have strengthened
media outlets, increased the capacity to provide high-quality content, and improved legal and
regulatory frameworks in many contexts. As noted throughout this report, media development is
among the predominant IIR strategies currently employed by USAID and builds on decades of
experience from all regions where USAID works. Among the 23 activities covered by this
review, 15 included media development components. Implementing partners employ well-
developed strategies that have been tested and refined over many years. As described below,
the research team observed clear evidence of effectiveness for activities implemented in diverse
contexts, including but not limited to Ukraine, Serbia, and the Democratic Republic of the
Congo.
At the sametime, we note that media development activities historically have not defined their
goals in terms of countering MDM, and there is disagreement among USAID and IP staff about
whether media development activities can or should do so. Thus, the Media Program in Ukraine
explicitly aims to counter MDM indirectly by improving the overall information ecosystem. Other
activities, including in Tanzania, Serbia, and Nicaragua, do not explicitly include countering
MDM as a project objective. A priority for USAID going forward will be to continue internal
discussion about whether and how the Agency relates media development to MDM
programming, and to invest in studying the effectiveness of such activities in building societal
resilience to MDM.
Second, there is also a substantial evidence base for activities in Category 2: Improving
Citizen Engagement with Media. Media literacy and public education activities, in particular,
have been shown to help citizens become critical consumers of media and avoid non-credible
information sources. As described below, several activities in this review offer evidence of
effectiveness, including in Ukraine, where national-level surveys suggest the activity has

contributed to increased public ability to identify credible news sources and may have
contributed to a decline in consumption of Russian-backed media—though we caution that it is
difficult to isolate project effects from other factors that may have influenced this shift. An
important caveat from academic literature is that not all types of media literacy are created
equal: teaching verification skills appears to be much more effective for building resilience
against online falsehoods than for understanding of digital technology, the media industry, or
journalistic ethics. USAID's media literacy activities employ a wide range of approaches, and the
agency should prioritize those shown to be most impactful.
For fact-checking, the evidence base is more limited, in part because relatively few activities in
the review included substantial fact-checking components, and the available M&E data focuses
on outputs, like the number of items debunked or reports produced, not higher-order impacts
related to citizen consumption or internalization of misinformation. KII respondents held mixed
views on whether fact-checking should be a core investment for USAID.
Third, for activities in Categories 3 - 5, the evidence base is limited. This stems in part
from the fact that some interventions in these categories reflect newer, innovative approaches
that have not been studied as extensively as more well-established strategies. In addition, as
noted in the Limitations section above, this review included only a small number of activities in
these categories, limiting the team's ability to identify common themes. For Category 3:
Understanding, Exposing, and Reacting to MDM, examples from Georgia, Ukraine, and the
global Civil Society Innovation Initiative show how research and monitoring can inform other
activity areas by assessing the professionalism of a country's media sector, identifying
underserved audiences, and tracking disinformation narratives over time. However, project
indicators typically do not measure how these research outputs affect broader IIR goals. For
Category 4: Strategic Communications, available evidence comes mainly from the Georgia
Information Integrity Project and suggests that communications campaigns produced jointly with
civil society partners attract positive public attention, though more time and study is needed to
evaluate whether they produce lasting change. For Category 5: Information Resilience Hubs,
country, regional, and global activities suggest that this approach can be a significant force
multiplier by bringing civil society organizations together, connecting them to practical research,
and encouraging them to design collaborative activities that advance shared objectives. But
those joint activities must be evaluated independently of the hub responsible for them.
Indicators measuring the number of collaborative activities completed, for instance, say little
about effects on the ground.
The next two sub-sections provide an extended discussion of Categories 1 and 2, for which
more evidence is available. Following that a sub-section covers other types of activities for
which there is less evidence. Next, we explore how behavior change approaches can improve
the way objectives are designed and measured to inform future program design, drawing on
insights from USAID public health activities. Finally, we discuss contextual factors related to
program design and assessment.

Summary of Accomplishments
Activities in this category have demonstrated the ability to strengthen the professionalism,
sustainability, accessibility, and independence of media systems and individual outlets. By doing
so, activities in this category promote resilience, either by providing high-integrity news and
information or by helping consumers access news and information despite of attempts at
manipulation. This is a familiar, longstanding set of priorities for USAID programming which has
relevance today, with some adaptations. It is less clear if these results go on to limit the impact
of low-integrity information by promoting healthy civic behavior, and it remains to be measured
whether they prevent or minimize avoidable harms from information manipulation.
Examples of success come from several activities, including the following:
• The Media Program in Ukraine assisted eighteen local and regional media outlets in
their transition from state-run media to publicly funded media.? With USAID support,
Ukrainian Civil Society also successfully advocated for reforms to the Ukrainian national
public broadcaster and against proposed legislation that would have hampered media
freedom.
• In Serbia, the Strengthening Media Systems program tracks the revenue and audience
growth of small local outlets who transitioned from government and grant funding to
more commercially viable models of journalism. For every dollar in grant support,
grantees generated $1.50 in revenue from subscriptions, crowdfunding, and other
sources. Grantees also reached larger audiences. For example, after the IP helped
rebuild the web portal for an outlet called Danas, it attracted roughly 20 million monthly
page views, making it among the top fifteen digital news sources in the country.
• In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, radio stations that received USAID-supported
trainings were rated as more professional by their listeners. Monitoring and evaluation
data found that in 2023, 49 percent of content produced by radio partners met
professional standards, up from 22 percent two years earlier.

These accomplishments contribute to the creation and development of independent, high-
quality media. However, as noted above, the current evidence base is insufficiently developed
to allow firm conclusions of whether such achievements lessen the effects of MDM—including in
relation to harms inferred from the TOCs for activities in this review, such as:
• foreign malign influence,
• intolerance,
• lack of citizen participation,
• social division and polarization,

The information literacy approach is similar to IREX's Learn to Discern methodology, which was
praised by interviewees and referenced in documents for multiple activities (including the AML
in Indonesia, which modeled its own content after Learn to Discern). In evaluations, participants
in Learn to Discern showed significant, durable gains in their ability to assess sources and
identify low-integrity information. Interviewees described IREX's evaluation approach as best-in-
class.2 Yet, it is important to note that Learn to Discern is primarily geared toward helping
individuals recognize MDM so they can seek out other sources. This goal is distinct from other
common objectives across USAID activities. For example, the Media Initiatives and Partnership
Support (MIPS) program in Serbia aims to educate citizens about the "complex media and
information landscape," including knowledge of the workings of journalism and digital
technology.
Future USAID activities should carefully consider the range of media literacy strategies and how
their impact is measured. Broad surveys are imprecise tools for tracking specific behavior
changes like consumption of content from specific propaganda outlets or decisions to share (or
not share) false information online. Delivery mechanisms should also be tested more
thoroughly. Implementers in Klls noted that while getting media literacy into school classrooms
can be a major achievement, it can be harder to provide these skills to busy adults. For this
reason, IPs have experimented with games, virtual reality exhibits, and public art displays to
engage the wider public. However, to date there is limited evidence on whether these strategies
are effective.

Understanding, Exposing, and Reacting to MDM. Activities such as media-monitoring, open-
source investigation of MDM, and other forms of research rarely include their own evidence of
success beyond simple output indicators. Most often, they are used to inform and evaluate other

the health of the overall media ecosystem in most countries, USAID could explore how to

Strategic Communications. As mentioned above, most evidence available for this category

MDM narratives which civil society could work to address through strategic communications

In Klls, USAID staff and partners stressed that these approaches require flexibility and speed.
Public discourse shifts quickly, and insights from audience research go stale fast. Interview

example of a video message featuring a celebrity urging people to stay indoors during the
pandemic—from the bedroom of their mansion.
Some USAID staff expressed concern that strategic communications might not fall under
USAID's development mandate. USAID should take up this question at a high level. If the
Agency does invest more in strategic communications programs, it should evaluate their
persuasive potential and second-order effects on governance and IIR. At present, IPs capture
important information through qualitative analysis, but that information is not always
incorporated in MERL plans. A better approach would draw a line from reach of content, through

The Importance of Local Context
The challenge is compounded by outstanding answers to key questions, many of which depend
on local context. Research into these issues can be counterintuitive: interview participants cited

disproved their assumptions about who shares MDM and why—but these findings may not
apply in other contexts.

Because there are some similarities between contexts, interview participants were eager to
trade observations with others, but cautioned against establishing best practices expected to be
applied universally.
Media development activities provided several examples of how context matters for program
success. In Serbia, interview participants said that pursuing regulatory reform was a low-impact
strategy. Rather, the lack of business fundamentals among local independent media was seen
as a bigger challenge than legal or regulatory restrictions on media. In Serbia, rules around
things like licensing are not the primary mechanism for government control of information;
access to capital is a more powerful and more commonly used means. Years of dependence on
grants meant that media outlets often had little working experience building subscription bases,
and state capture of advertising and other sources of finance led to an unfair media market
across the country. However, in Ukraine USAID activities demonstrated concrete gains in the
legal and regulatory environment that furthered goals of reforming a media apparatus that still
bears the imprint of the Soviet era, particularly state ownership of media.
Another example came from Nicaragua, where almost all independent media is now in exile.
USAID works with these outlets to help them professionalize and establish credibility with
audiences wary and cynical after years of propaganda. Past assessments of USAID activities

Even though geographic and political context can be constricting, cross-country learning is not
fruitless or impossible. Assessing which best practices are truly "best" in a given place,
however, requires sensitivity to local context.
8. CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS
Conclusion
The USAID activities assessed in this report are caught in a crosswind. Many of the 23 activities
included here started long before 2018, when the Agency began considering responses to MDM
an urgent U.S. government priority, according to several interviewees. As a result, some
activities conceived as straightforward media development activities are expected to also be
responsive to MDM—though their original objectives, TOCs, and evaluation approaches do not
reflect this goal. At the same time, some U.S. government analysis and outside observers
question the wisdom of "reactive" strategies to counter MDM, advocating instead for broader
efforts to create resilient media environments less vulnerable to political manipulation and more
conducive to vibrant, pluralistic democratic societies. "Legacy" media development activities fit
this mold, even if it is difficult to use currently available evidence to draw direct causal lines
between their objectives and the diminished impact of MDM.
As noted throughout this report, some USAID staff expressed concerns that support for the
media sector might be "instrumentalized" as efforts to counter the influence of actors opposed to
U.S. policy goals. Going forward, USAID should explore which types of IIR activities are within
its mandate and guiding ethos as a development agency. Others held similar concerns about
the use of strategic communications to support democracy and governance objectives-though
activities under the Office of Transitions Initiatives and public health also recognize the
importance of communications, identity, and social relationships in mitigating harms from MDM.
During the same period, parts of USAID have begun experimenting with novel responses to
MDM. The Georgia Information Integrity Project stands out for its distinct use of strategic

communications to provide alternative narratives to vulnerable audiences—promoting social

These two streams of activity are united under this report, but they respond to a complex
challenge in different ways. USAID has not reached consensus on the most appropriate way to
pursue information resilience objectives—be it through media development, citizen education,
strategic communications, or some other combination of approaches. Without this strategic
clarity, the combination of shifting priorities and novel approaches often renders evidence for
impact on IIR and MDM suggestive at best. In future rounds of program design, USAID should
reevaluate where in the Agency responsibility for IIR and MDM lies, which activities aim
explicitly to address these concerns, which have other goals like media development or social
cohesion, and how to best design monitoring, evaluation, research, and learning agendas that
can provide more definitive answers about effectiveness.
This report concludes with a set of programmatic and MERL recommendations to assist in this
process. As noted in the in the introduction, the order of the recommendations generally follows
the structure of the report and is not meant to convey that some recommendations are more
important than others.
Programmatic Recommendations
1. Make long-term investments in information integrity and resilience while pursuing
short-term harm mitigation. USAID must be able to pursue both long-term change and
rapid responses to emerging threats simultaneously. Whether short- or long-term
approaches are most appropriate will depend on specific program objectives and contexts.
For example, during elections, on-going conflicts, or crisis situations, a generational program
to improve government accountability is not responsive to pressing needs. In these
situations, USAID should have a ready set of short-term approaches to mitigate the risk of
serious harms. More generally, however, USAID should invest in longer-term efforts to
strengthen media environments and improve how citizens navigate information landscapes,
building resilience to future shocks and challenges. Some activities, including strategio
communications capacity building, can address both short- and long-term objectives at the
same time: by enhancing civil society's ability to influence public discourse through values-
based messaging, USAID activities can promote long-term infrastructure used for advocacy
of democratic values while also addressing more immediate threats.
2. Continue pursuing media development objectives independent of the IIR agenda-but
where appropriate, tie those activities to IIR-related goals and indicators. Media
development activities have demonstrated positive effects on indicators related to their
longstanding objectives: they can quantify, for example, increases in revenue after adoption
of best practices or improvements in the perceived credibility of news content. However, as
noted in the previous recommendation, they do not typically measure whether investments
in independent media produce follow-on benefits by counteracting harms from MDM related
to civic participation, social cohesion, or societal distrust. A robust independent media is
necessary but not sufficient for information resilience. If USAID activities want media

3. Prioritize testing and refining media literacy approaches. Media literacy and public
education are common components of IIR activities. As described in Section 4, the review
found that 43 percent (10 of 23) of activities included such components. Both USAID MERL
data and academic literature suggest that media literacy can be effective at reducing the
audience and impact of low-integrity information." However, few USAID activities are set up
to assess whether the provision of media literacy education leads to enduring changes in
behavior like verifying source credibility or avoiding untrustworthy outlets. An exception is
the Advancing Media Literacy project in Indonesia, which iteratively tests and improves
digital media literacy campaign strategies and publishes the results in scholarly journals.
The content of curricula also varies widely. Existing literature provides many competing
variants of "media literacy" and suggests that information literacy specifically is important for
resilience against MDM. Given the prominence and promise of this intervention type, greater
resources should be devoted to studying the effectiveness of differing media literacy
approaches, curricula, and delivery mechanisms, with programmatic refinements made
based on the evolving evidence base.
The need for additional testing of core strategies has been noted in some activity
documentation. For example, the mid-term evaluation for the Media Program in Ukraine
noted that,
, "In order to independently verify whether ML [media literacy] efforts actually
increased citizens' abilities to determine quality information and to consume more high-
quality content, it would be necessary to study citizens who have been reached by MPU ML
activities, rather than the journalism professionals who were interviewed or surveyed for this
evaluation. Even in a mass survey, the issue of the link between ML efforts and any
changes in the mass data would be elusive without an experimental setup comparing control
and treatment groups." Likewise, in Indonesia, the Advancing Media Literacy for New Digital
Arrivals in Developing Countries FY 2022 first quarterly progress report reached similar
conclusions. Moonshot, one of the implementing partners, wrote that it is planning a "series
of experiments" on media literacy to "establish a more accurate measurement for behavioral
and attitudinal change."
Media literacy activities should be evaluated not just with national surveys or post-training
test scores but also with approaches that measure whether conveyed skills make a
difference in the daily lives of citizens and their communities over time. This can be more
difficult to measure-the midterm evaluation for the MPU above indicates more scientific
approaches like longitudinal studies and RCTs, which can be expensive and complex-but
the effect on individuals experiencing the intervention is the ultimate test of impact. It is also
important to avoid self-assessments as a metric for media and information literacy.

4. Consider whether and how to proceed with strategic communications activities
designed to counter MDM in the political sphere. Despite the promise of strategic
communications activities, few activities included in this review adopt this strategy. USAID
should pause to consider whether and how it wants to proceed in this area of programming,
which carries both promise and risk. In doing so, it should emphasize collecting more
evidence of impact. As noted, the limited number of activities of this type included in this
review makes it difficult to adequately assess this approach.
The strategic communications campaigns under GlIP are among the more innovative
activities reviewed for this report. Disinformation often involves narratives, beliefs, and social
divisions that are subjective and non-falsifiable; strategic communications are an
appropriate way of addressing these issues. For example, the GIIP program attempted to
create economic links between Tbilisi and regions of Georgia that felt economically isolated
and exposed to a hostile Russia—addressing the sort of social divisions and economic
inequities that make societies vulnerable to disinformation in the first place.
While USAID teams working in public health and conflict resolution often use strategic
communications and counter-messaging activities in their work, this review found some
hesitance to do so for IIR activities. In an interview, one USAID staffer involved with the GlIP
said it could be characterized as promoting attitudinal change; they expected, but to date
have not heard, concerns that it is out of scope for USAID and more befitting a State
Department public diplomacy program. Some DRG implementing partners also described
discomfort with the notion of pursing behavior and attitudinal change in their work. In an
interview, one USAID staffer also expressed concerns that "counternarratives" are not
effective, raising the possibility that to justify investments in strategic communications
activities, "alternative narratives" must be sufficiently distinct from attempts to merely present
USG perspectives more assertively in the face of adversarial propaganda.
5. Fund iterative, experimental activities designed to generate insights for future
activities. USAID should support activities designed to test and iterate upon common
approaches to fill crucial knowledge gaps. These might be shorter term initiatives, or they
might be longer activities designed to include multiple iterative cycles. For example, USAID
could explore the most effective ways to deliver media literacy training to adults outside the
classroom through an iterative, adaptive program in one or more countriesborrowing
insights from the Advancing Media Literacy project in Indonesia.
USAID's Office of Transitions Initiatives runs activities on significantly shorter timeframes
than most USAID teams; timelines are measured in months, not years, and include frequent
pauses to reflect, assess, learn, and adapt. This iterative process treats research and
practice as a loop in which each component continually informs and supports the other.

this means making TOCs more narrow, achievable, and measurable by including a series of
more modest, discrete steps that can be completed in the allotted timeframe and with the
available resources. Activities without a formal TOC should also develop specific,
achievable, and attributable objectives that reflect project timelines and the scope of
activities. While this recommendation relates to MERL approaches, it is also important at the
program design stage.
USAID activities are often developed and renewed on five-year cycles, but many
interviewees described the changes they hoped to achieve as generational. TOCs often
include "then" statements with lofty macro-social goals like more accountable government,
social stability, or resilience against attempts to undermine democracy - outcomes that
typically cannot be realized on a five-year cycle. TOCs should include a series of more
modest discrete steps that can be achieved and measured in the allotted timeframe. It may
be the case that the ultimate objective is still generational change, and activities may even
stipulate this in writing—but it should be made clear how each iteration of a five-year
program will incrementally contribute toward the envisioned end goal.

in this review incorporate GESI considerations in program designs in meaningful ways.
USAID and IPs should think about 1) whether programming should more directly address
harms specific to women and marginalized groups; 2) whether and how existing activities
impact these groups differently than men and people from non-marginalized groups; and 3)

MERL Recommendations
9. USAID should increase resources for a broad set of MERL approaches for IIR
activities to expand the evidence base on what works. The biggest modifiable challenge
related to assessing the impact of activities is a lack of resources, including funds, time, and
staff. USAID should prioritize funding MERL and should expand the use of both qualitative
and quantitative strategies as part of routine M&E conducted by IPs and through the greater
use of independent evaluations and research. USAID should integrate research efforts into
project M&E plans, with the goal of generating findings that can be shared with others
working on IIR programming. The agency should also invest in independent research and
evaluations that complement project M&E approaches. A useful target would be to dedicate
a minimum of 5 percent of each program's budget to monitoring, internal evaluation, and
learning.3 In addition, USAID should plan to set aside funding for external evaluations,
including performance and impact evaluations for a subset of high-priority activities that are
amenable to these approaches (see recommendation 13 below on impact evaluations).
Beyond funding, USAID should also recognize the time required to design and implement
high-quality MERL plans and allow activities more flexibility for program learning and
adaptation. Finally, USAID can encourage IPs to update TOCs and results frameworks as
they adapt their programming.
10. Consider funding multi-project evaluations to expand the evidence base for priority
activity areas. As noted in Finding 12, the evidence base for newer, innovative approaches
is more limited. For priority areas where USAID needs to develop deeper understanding of
effectiveness, the agency should fund evaluations that employ research designs that are
beyond the scope of this review. For example, USAID could fund an evaluation that
examines a specific intervention type, such as fact-checking or strategic communications.

11. USAID and IPs should consider increased usage of complexity-aware MERL
strategies. Activities facing high uncertainty and that aim to quickly test interventions,
adapt, and iterate can benefit from MERL systems that adapt with the activity. This means
reducing the size and burden of theory-based MERL systems to allow time and resources
for complexity-aware and flexible approaches.
Often when considering about complexity-aware approaches, people think about data
collection methods, like outcome harvesting or most significant change. Although these
methods can be used in complexity-aware ways, CAMEL is first and foremost a set of
principles that guide the way activities use MERL. These principles include:
1. Attend to the blind spots of program theory-based monitoring and evaluation. Identify
and assess uncertain and unpredictable cause and effect relationships in the project
logic model.
2. Monitor systemically (interrelationships, perspectives, and boundaries).
3. Synchronize MEL with the pace of change.
CAMEL is particularly appropriate when:
• There are uncertain and unpredictable cause and effect relationships in the project
logic model.
• A project is subject to influence by contextual factors.
• A project is likely to contribute to emergent (unpredictable) outcomes.
• Stakeholders bring diverse perspectives; goals and strategies are contested; and
consensus is impractical.
• The pace of change is dynamic, and changes in the context lead to new
opportunities and needs.
• Adaptive management is necessary to effectively implement an activity.
Activities will always have limited resources and will need to prioritize what they monitor.
Most activities will have some parts of the program that are particularly sensitive to
complexity and others that are not. When prioritizing what and how to monitor, USAID and
IPs should use CAMEL approaches to monitor the aspects of the program that are sensitive
to complexity and theory-based MERL approaches (e.g., indicators) to monitor the parts of
the program were uncertainty is lower.

in recommendation 5 above, USAID should consider expanding flexible, iterative program

13. USAID should increase the use of impact evaluation methods for some types of
activities. Impact evaluations based on RCTs are the gold standard for evaluating program
impacts. Building a stronger evidence base will require selectively identifying opportunities
for using RCTs as part of a broad suite of monitoring and evaluation strategies. RCTs
should complement, not replace, routine monitoring and performance evaluation strategies
that are critical for tracking project implementation and learning lessons through other data
collection methods.
RCTs have several well-known limitations: they are costly and time consuming; they are not
appropriate for some types of activities and contexts; they are difficult to implement and
sometimes fail due to non-compliance with the randomization protocol; and they sometimes
do not produce actionable insights. Despite these limitations, it is critical to include RCTs as
part of a broad set of M&E strategies for learning about what works (and what doesn't) in
building resilient information ecosystems. However, in our document review, we identified
only a single RCT-based evaluation in the 23 activities examined (for a journalist training
activity in Tanzania34).
RCTs are most useful and appropriate for interventions that meet three criteria. First, the
activity type is being (or has the potential to be) implemented in multiple countries. For
activities that are specific to a small number of countries or distinct contexts, there is
generally less value in conducting RCT-based evaluations since the results will not have
relevance to a large set of countries. Second, the intervention must be amenable to a
randomized implementation approach that creates control and treatment groups. Some
types of activities are not appropriate because there are not enough participants to allow for
this division or it would be contrary to program goals to exclude some individuals or
organizations to create a control group. Third, RCTs are most useful when there is a limited
or mixed evidence base for an intervention, either because there is a lack of prior research,
previous findings are mixed, or there is considerable skepticism about its efficacy within
USAID or IPs.
In our assessment, all USAID-funded activities included in this review have widespread
usages (or potential usage) and would be amenable to an RCT-based approach (at least for
some project components). Table 3 identifies the four interventions that meet the other two
criteria, making them most suitable for RCT-based impact evaluations. First, activities that
provide support for independent high-quality content frequently include a journalist training
component with a large number of participants, potentially allowing for a randomized
implementation plan. Moreover, the Tanzania RCT-based study mentioned above found that
the training program had no measurable effect on key outcomes, suggesting a need for
additional research. Third, the literature review found limited evidence that media literacy

Furthermore, they can conduct content analysis on comments to see 1) if women and
