15. National opinion surveys in most cases should not be used for outcome indicators.
National opinion surveys are valuable for understanding baseline attitudes and behaviors
and tracking their evolution over time. However, national opinion surveys are typically not
appropriate for use as outcome indicators, since it usually impossible to attribute shifts in
national-level data on views and behaviors to project activities, separate from the multitude
of other influences.
There are at least three challenges related to survey-based outcome indicators. First, even
the most successful activities generally produce small marginal changes in attitudes and
behaviors that may be too small to be detected in nationally representative surveys of 1,000
to 1,200 respondents (the typical sample size for many surveys). Small changes (positive or
negative) in self-reported attitudes and behaviors from one survey to the next are likely to be
attributable to random variation between survey samples, rather than statistically significant
shifts. Second, survey-based measures are subject to response biases that may be difficult
to detect. For example, short-term changes in self-reported media consumption data could
reflect shifting perceptions about the social desirability of "admitting" which media sources
respondents consume. Also, shifting contextual factors can affect self-assessments of
media literacy skills, as noted in Klls with respondents in Serbia. Third, and most important,
it is typically not possible to isolate the effect of USAID-funded activities on national-level
measures of attitudes and behaviors from surveys. Doing so requires identifying and
accounting for the myriad other factors that influence these measures, which is usually not
possible. Due to this attribution problem, USAID should discourage IPs from using survey-
based measures as outcome indicators.
16. Content reach is not a strong outcome indicator and should be coupled with other
strategies for assessing audience impact, when possible. Many activities use audience
reach indicators as evidence of program effects. While reach is important, it is only the first
step in achieving meaningful effects related to project goals in many cases. On its own,
reach says little about audience reaction or uptake of messages. For some activities like

CONTEXT
In 2013, the Euromaidan protests (sometimes called the "revolution of dignity") led to the exile of
former Ukrainian President Yanukovych and the election of a new government. It decidedly
changed the country's political course and orientation, shifting it toward European integration.
But the next year, Ukraine's post-revolutionary hardships were compounded by the Russian
seizure of the Crimean Peninsula and stoking of separatist rebellions in Ukraine's east and
south. This military crisis was accompanied by a media blitz on Russian state television and
over social media, which frequently repeated false narratives about Ukrainian reprisals against
ethnic Russians and a "Nazi regime" in Kyiv. Because of this, the 2014 start of the Russo-
Ukrainian conflict is sometimes seen as a revolution in information warfare.
These momentous challenges arose in the context of a former Soviet republic where wealthy
oligarchs owned and operated media outlets as instruments of political influence. Truly
independent media was difficult to sustain—both financially and because of violence against
journalists by the state and organized criminal actors.
USAID and other development agencies have a long history of working to improve Ukraine's
media environment. The Media Program in Ukraine (MPU) builds on decades of work to
improve media sustainability, democratic accountability, and good governance in Ukraine."
Interview participants reported that commitment lapsed following the Orange Revolution, when
Ukraine rejected attempts to steal the Presidential election for the pro-Russian and notoriously
corrupt Viktor Yanukovych. The Orange Revolution was seen as a major political opening for
reform, but instead it led to political infighting and stagnation. During this period, many donors
reduced their support to Ukrainian media. The country's upward trajectory was reversed after

Yanukovych's successful 2010 election campaign. After his ouster, Ukrainian civil society and
international donors saw a new window for reform, and investment in Ukraine again increased.
Since then, Ukraine has had to juggle two enormous tasks: fending off the aggression of a much
larger neighboring state and implementing democratic reforms, including in the media sector,
while dealing with endemic corruption. The results have been impressive and include the
replacement of much of the old police force, the conversion of state media into public
broadcasters, and legal reforms including new laws related to transparency of media ownership,
access to public information, and the conversion of the national state television broadcaster into
a public service entity.
THEORY OF CHANGE & OBJECTIVES
The Media Program in Ukraine promotes information resilience by advocating for reforms to
media laws, improving the environment for sustainable media, helping news outlets
professionalize, and encouraging media literacy across the population. These efforts continue
against the backdrop of full-scale warfare following the February 2022 Russian invasion aimed
at overthrowing Ukraine's government. Journalists continue their work, covering the battlefield
with help from training and equipment provided by USAID partners.
Program documents describe the MPU as designed to "strengthen the civically relevant role of
media in democratic processes in Ukraine, and expand citizens' access to quality information in
order to counter malign influence and support European integration." In Klls, IP staff said that
instead of a theory of change, they base their work on a "development hypothesis":
"IF transformational media reforms are implemented, high-quality, engaging content is
increased, public demand for quality journalism grows, and self-governance of the sector
improves,
THEN the civically relevant role of media will be strengthened and citizens will be
equipped with quality information that counters malign influence and supports European
integration."
Initially, the MPU's objectives were 1) Corruption Reduced in Target Sector, 2) Impacts of
Russian Aggression Mitigated, 3) Democratic Governance Strengthened, and 4) Inclusive,
Sustainable Market-Driven Economic Growth.
Following the escalation of the war between Russia and Ukraine in 2022, the program was
extended to 2025 with four new objectives:
1) Increase high-quality, engaging content throughout Ukraine, particularly in the east and
south;
2) Increase public demand for quality information;
3) Implement critical media reforms; and
4) Strengthen and sustain key media institutions and processes.

These objectives imply a relationship between the supply of high-integrity information and publio

public media literacy skills so citizens can seek out high-quality news and reject sources of
MDM, thereby providing expanded audiences for USAID-supported outlets producing high-
quality, objective journalism. USAID also helps grow that supply both by assisting outlets
directly via training and subgrants and by pursuing legal advocacy around improvements in the
enabling environment for media.
PROGRAM ACTIVITIES
Internews, the implementing partner for the MPU, sub-grants a minimum of half the activity
budget to local partners to carry out a wide variety of initiatives. Most activities target journalists,
news outlets, and the media sector broadly. The MPU also supports activities that use public art
and other means of reaching the public and provides training to media professionals on various
topics.
In 2022, 49 sub-grants were awarded. One went to Internews Ukraine (not to be confused with
Internews, the main IP for this project), which received $1.6 million to promote "critical media
consumption" among the Ukrainian public and work with journalists to support coverage of
government reforms. It also provided digital security training to Ukrainian journalists, who face
persistent cyber threats from Russian intelligence services and other actors.
Detektor Media received more than one million dollars, part of which was spent monitoring
Ukrainian news media for its level of professionalism and providing media literacy education to
citizens. Detektor also supported advocacy for media sector reforms. It continues monitoring
Ukrainian TV outlets as other institutions—the Pylyp Orlyk Institute for Democracy and the
Volyn Press Club—monitor digital and print media.
The National Association of Media received $779,000 to work with regional broadcast outlets to
improve the quality of their content. It also provided legal support to journalists, delivered
management trainings for media personnel, and conducted advocacy campaigns supporting
media reforms, including destatization of television outlets.
Some efforts related to media literacy show a distinct level of creativity, especially those made
during the COVID-19 pandemic. For example, an online comedy outlet, Toronto TV, produced
twelve videos and more than 200 posts on Instagram promoting media literacy. Internews
Ukraine created a "propagandarium" exhibit to promote media literacy in a more engaging
format. In classrooms, USAID partners created games promoting media literacy and worked to
integrate media literacy training into more than 360 educational institutions.
Support for investigative journalism is an important component of MPU's efforts to support the
creation of independent content and reduce corruption. One example comes from March 2021,
when a partner outlet called Bihus.info produced an episode of its YouTube show,
"Unscammed," exposing a bribery scheme in the Ukrainian Navy. Sailors were being asked to
pay illegal "registration fees" to officials in exchange for a passing examination grade. After

GENDER / MARGINALIZED COMMUNITIES
The activities and objectives under this program only occasionally focus on gender or
marginalized communities. MERL indicators also do not relate much to GESI issues. An
exception is the percent of experts quoted in news content who are women.
Program documents provide some success stories like OstroV, a media outlet which conducted
a nine-month media campaign to raise awareness of gender issues. After the campaign, the
female share of OstroV's audience grew from 36% to 53%, and a majority of its journalists
committed to featuring more expert comments from women and to continue covering issues
affecting women.
Most of the examples of gender-sensitive programming from the MPU showcase improvements
in media coverage and journalistic working conditions. One participant in a gender awareness
training for media praised these efforts, saying:
"Before I started a gender column and dove deeper into the topic, I did not know
much about the topic of gender sensitivity. Because I used to think something
like this: the inequality of our rights is not critical, it is not the Taliban, after all, so
my voice is not very important here...l was bitterly mistaken, first, about the scale
of the problem, and second, about the insignificance of my voice in this choir. So
don't do [as I did]...start speaking about inequality of women's rights in Ukraine
now."
The MPU could go further in its focus on gender rights. In Klls, USAID staff suggested that
activities could more meaningfully design for and measure gender-related outcomes by asking
how the problems in their theory ofchange uniquely effect women and marginalized groups,
then measuring change over time. The MPU might consider doing this by using indicators and
qualitative assessments such as focus groups to determine if, for example, gendered narratives
in media (and especially disinformation) diminish after exposure to USAID-supported activities.
MERL APPROACHES
With the exception of mitigating the impacts of Russian aggression, the initial objectives for the
MPU do not speak directly to countering MDM or even fostering information resilience. Rather,
they make a core assumption about the role of journalism in a democratic society and pursue a
wide range of activities intended to improve the media sector's ability to play that role in
Ukraine. While this might fall under the umbrella of "information resilience," MERL plans and
indicators are not designed with this framework in mind.
The MPU's MELP Plan makes use of twenty indicators. Some of these are simple output
indicators, such as the number of journalists trained and supported (3,399, as of reporting
period FY2022). More were outcome indicators—but often, these were difficult to causally

The MPU also tracks reported consumption of Russian media through surveys. In the earlier
years of the project, a noteworthy percentage of Ukrainians reported consuming Russian media
or knowing people who did. Their reasons for doing so were not always based on trust,
however—a little more than a third said they did so to see what Russian media was saying
about the conflict. Over the course of the conflict, consumption of Russian media has fallen
significantly, as has professed trust in that media. But it is difficult to credit this solely to USAID
efforts; the war has surely exercised its own independent impact on Ukrainian appetites for
Russian news, as has Kyiv's 2017 ban on Russian social media networks (social media pages
were the most frequent source of Russian news reported in the survey).
A new MERL plan drafted in 2022 for the next phase of the project shows a continued focus on
sustaining and improving journalism in Ukraine. Specifically, it aims to evaluate:
• To what extent is MPU contributing to better journalism practices in Ukraine?
• To what extent is MPU contributing to increasing trust in balanced, evidence-based
information sources, especially in the East and South?
The emphasis on the East and South is significant, since these regions are historically more
vulnerable to Russian manipulation and more distrustful of Kyiv and the West. Donetsk and
Luhansk, the two cities occupied by Russia before 2022, are in Ukraine's East, and the early
days of the conflict in 2014 saw violence in cities like Kharkiv, Odessa, and Mariupol. The focus
here indicates sustained intent to build information resilience, even if MERL indicators are not
directly tied to this implicit goal.

Taken together, the evidence for MPU's impact is impressive overall but inconclusive in key
areas. In 2022, the Cloudburst Group conducted a mid-term evaluation of the MPU using a

determine which activities were working and what could be improved. It found that the program
led to improvements in Ukraine's media landscape and that its efforts to train and equip
journalists were praised by recipients. However, IPs struggled to attract new entrants to the field
of journalism and to promote collaboration across regional media. Disinformation remains a
major, even growing, problem in Ukraine despite efforts to counter it, and the evaluation was not

CONTEXT
While the Rose Revolution in 2003 put Georgia on a trajectory toward EU and NATO accession,
the current government has drifted from that course. Despite the 2008 Russo-Georgian war and
the continuing Russian occupation of a fifth of Georgia's territory, the ruling Georgian Dream
party remains skeptical of NATO membership and prefers a more nuanced relationship with
Moscow.
Georgia's information environment is heavily afflicted by MDM, much of which stokes fear about
conflict with Russia and the consequences of EU membership for traditional conservative
Georgians. While Russia may have once been the main source of low-integrity information in
Georgia, today the Georgian government echoes many of Moscow's talking points in its own
communications. As a result, many of the reform-oriented approaches applied by USAID
partners in other contexts are less feasible in Georgia, where government partnership is more
difficult. Instead, USAID and its partners are implementing what is by far the most heavily
communications focused project reviewed for this report. In conjunction with local civil society
organizations, the IP for this project has planned and executed social media and other
messaging campaigns designed to increase social cohesion, patriotism, national unity, and
awareness of disinformation narratives about the war in Ukraine and other issues.
THEORY OF CHANGE & OBJECTIVES
The theory of change for the Georgia Information Integrity Project (GIIP) reflects its conception
as an information resilience hub—a networking center that provides knowledge, resources, and
capacity building to a network of local partners. It reads:

disinformation ecosystem in Georgia;
AND IF: the project can bring together a diverse network of private and public sector
actors across Georgia, building their capacity to work collectively to develop and test
responses to disinformation identified through the ecosystem map,

The program also supported three investigations: one into Russian capital in Georgian
businesses, a second into the financial ties of far-right groups in Georgia, and a third mapping
the offline influence of pro-Kremlin actors in Georgia.
The GIIP's design sprints develop communications campaigns, for example around reclaiming
patriotic Georgian symbols from the far right or combatting Soviet nostalgia by pointing to
alternative sources of civic pride in the city of Gori, Stalin's birthplace. The design sprints also
develop tools, like the first software that recognizes the Georgian alphabet in PDFs and can
transform them into editable text. These tools were eligible for accelerator grants to help
develop them further.
GENDER / MARGINALIZED COMMUNITIES
Other than the number of female journalists trained, program documents provided little evidence
of GESI indicators or approaches. Kll participants said that they do not consider these issues
urgent because "information affects everyone no matter their gender." They pointed to audience
research showing that gender does not make a marked difference in vulnerability to
disinformation.
However, respondents acknowledged that female candidates are more likely to be the target of
disinformation during elections. They also said that issues related to gender norms, gender
identity, and sexuality are often the topic of Russian propaganda narratives. And the GlIP noted
that in their work on COVID-19 vaccine misinformation, there was a strong push to make sure
both genders were reached with information.

MERL APPROACHES
The GIIP asks a series of key questions to assess progress toward program objectives. Are
audiences more aware of information integrity issues? Are key stakeholders responsive to
GIIP's investigations? Do GIIP partners reach and influence audiences, mitigate harm from
MDM, and promote "whole-of-society"
policies and approaches in this area?
Answers to some of these are captured by indicators. For example, the project uses surveys to
measure the percent of the target population who could identify MDM. The project also
measures the reach of its "learning products" produced for CSOs and the communications
campaigns aimed at the public, and tracks the number of partners it trains and the number of
investigations informed by the ecosystem map it developed with the Digital Forensic Research
Lab.
The program makes use of national surveys conducted quarterly (more recently, it has
produced an annual national survey and quarterly "deep dive" surveys). One of these, for
example, assessed vulnerability to MDM narratives by studying "information consumption
habits, attitudes towards western integration and towards Russia, as well as levels of agreement
with major disinformation and propaganda narratives."
In Klls, participants recognized that survey data and social media reach metrics alone cannot
demonstrate impact. For this reason, the program also uses a variety of qualitative tools. These
include focus groups and sentiment analysis of the comments and mentions associated with
GIIP-supported content.
To measure changes in the capacity of network partners, the IP asks partners to conduct self-
assessments following program activities. The results are combined with quarterly interviews
with network partners.
EVIDENCE OF EFFECTIVENESS
A key assessment challenge for the GIIP is going beyond demonstrating the reach of its
campaigns and connecting that reach to real change. Program documents provide some key
examples of this. For instance, the "Disinformation Dishonors Our Heroes" campaign reached
1.8 million social media impressions, and perhaps more tellingly, it earned media coverage from
45 outlets. When asked about the campaign, some politicians from the ruling party tried to
distance themselves from earlier statements supporting anti-Western narratives about the war in
Ukraine.
As the program evolves, it will hopefully rely less on national polls—changes in which are
difficult to attribute to any one factor—and emphasize measuring durable changes in behavior
and attitude that can be traced back to GIIP interventions. The project already uses qualitative

A/B testing and RCTs to rigorously test the effects of strategic messaging on audiences.
Experimental approaches could show, for example, whether people really bought more fruit
from border regions of Georgia or consumed less Russian media after seeing patriotic appeals.
The innovative tools and campaigns informed by the GIIP's design sprints could by themselves
be taken as a sign of success: Georgian civil society organizations came together to solve
problems and walked away with tools and action plans. The incorporation of artists and singers
was another innovation and success for GIIP; it reflects sentiments across USAID that

beyond familiar civil society activists.

A3. SERBIA
CONTEXT
Although Serbia's constitution guarantees freedom of the press, the country ranks 93 out of
180 countries on the 2021 World Freedom Press Index assembled by Reporters without
Borders. A variety of challenges deter media outlets from producing unbiased and timely
information. These include pressure from political and economic interests, threats to
independent journalists, out-of-date and unsustainable business models, and media funding
from the government that is used to influence private media. Surveys also show that almost half
of Serbian citizens say they do not trust the media.
Despite these challenges, more and more media outlets are registering in Serbia. There are
more than 2,600 media outlets officially operating in the country, and they have an advertising
market value of about $224 million. However, this still represents less than 25% of the total
media market, indicating that the majority of funding is available mostly to pro-government
media.
USAID Serbia has funded three activities with an information resilience and integrity component:
Media Initiatives and Partnership Support (MIPS); Media Innovation Activity (MI); and
Strengthening Media Systems (SMS). SMS, which ran from 2017-2022, was the predecessor to
Ml, which began in 2022 and is ongoing through 2027. Both activities were implemented by
IREX. SMS/MI focus on media development while MIPS focuses on media literacy. As no
activity lives on its own, these activities need to be viewed in the context of the overall USAID
Serbia portfolio. The three activities work together to build both the supply/sustainability of and
the demand for unbiased, independent media.

In the documents we reviewed, there was no information about MIPS's approach to addressing
GESI issues within their program. When asked about GESI approaches in an interview, staff
reported that they did not have a specific strategy related to inclusion. But mid-implementation,
their MEL team had a discussion related to issues of gender equality and how to collect gender
data, especially in their research activities, to better understand the complex issue of digital
literacy in Serbia.
MERL APPROACHES
The MIPS MERL plan includes 15 indicators designed to measure and assess progress on
established project objectives and tasks. The indicators include Media, Information and Digital
Literacy Indices (MIL and DIL Index), measured through annual surveys; four outcome
indicators; and 10 output indicators. Data are collected on areas such as self-reported
knowledge gains, number of reforms proposed, and number of people reached. Trainings are
evaluated through self-reported knowledge gains and other measures, such as analysis of
social media content for trained social media influencers. MIPS also collects qualitative data on
success stories; what media people use, how often, and why; and levels of trust and confidence
in the media.
MIPS uses the MEL data they collect to improve their activities, develop content for media
campaigns, and to attract new partners. For example, by sharing their success stories with the
public, MIPS garnered attention from some major social media companies who indicated in
interest in partnering with MIPS on social media campaigns.
EVIDENCE OF EFFECTIVENESS
Based on the documents reviewed, evidence of MIPS's success falls into three major
categories: increased skills of Serbian citizens to navigate a complex information landscape;
MIPS's social media reach; and results of trainings. Based on annual surveys on MDIL, MIPS

reviewed for this case study. This suggests that there is some improvement in Serbian citizens'
ability to navigate the information landscape, although the change is small, and there is
insufficient evidence to attribute the change to MIPS's activities.

CONTEXT
Indonesia is a large democracy with a rapidly increasing internet and social media user base.
Between 2015 and 20, the percent of the Indonesian population online grew 27 percentage
points, from 43% to 70%. By 2025 an estimated 82% of Indonesians will be online (Statista
2020). As of 2023, WhatsApp had an Indonesian penetration rate of 92%, and other social
media sites, such as Instagram and Facebook, also had high penetration rates.38
Unfortunately, this high social media usage leaves Indonesia vulnerable to online "hoaxes" (the
term used for misinformation in the Indonesian context) related to politics, religion, and other
newsworthy events. For example, in the 2019 national election, online disinformation created
significant division within the population.39 This led to violent protests against the election
results, resulting in six deaths. The Indonesian government temporarily suspended access to
social media platforms to try to quell the protests.4°
USAID Indonesia funds four activities with an information resilience and integrity component.
This case study is limited to two activities for which documents were available to the review
team: the MADANI Civil Society Support Initiative (MADANI) and Advancing Media Literacy
(AML). Both programs work to improve Indonesia's media literacy. MADANI works to improve
the way CSOs access and create content so that they can 1) become trusted sources of
information for their communities, 2) share their media literacy knowledge with those
communities, and 3) create alternate narratives to counter mis/disinformation. AML has created
a media literacy website and online game that is targeted directly to new internet users, who
may not have the media literacy skills needed to determine the trustworthiness of news sources.
They also conduct research to understand trends in online disinformation. They share their
findings with partners, who can decide if/how to address these disinformation campaigns.

THEORY OF CHANGE & OBJECTIVES
AML aims to improve media literacy in Indonesia. Their theory of change states that "IF we
provide customized online media literacy content to segmented audiences of new digital
arrivals, THEN the recipients of media literacy will be less likely to engage with and spread
misinformation." Specific objectives were not stated in the documents available to the review
team.
PROGRAM ACTIVITIES
AML engages in four types of activities. The first set of activities is related to digital media
forensics, or social media listening. This involves tracking the spread of misinformation,
conducting regular image manipulation forensics, developing and improving a Misinformation
Early Warning System (MEWS), and cultivating a media literacy ecosystem with local partners.
The second set of activities is related to the development, monitoring, and improvement of an
educational website (Literata.id) and game (Gali Fakta) to fight misinformation in Indonesia. The
third set of activities is related to the development, evaluation, and adaptation of media literacy
campaigns. Specifically, AML works with its partners to identify social media influencers who are
willing to share a media literacy message. AML gives them a particular media literacy lesson,
and the influencers find a creative way to share the message through short videos. Finally, the
fourth set of activities is related to partner capacity building and an eventual handoff of the
MEWS to a local partner that can sustain it.
GENDER / MARGINALIZED COMMUNITIES
In the documents we reviewed, there was no information about AML's approach to addressing
GESI issues within their program. When we spoke with program implementers, they
acknowledged that GESI is not a focus of their work but is something they consider. For
example,when selecting influencers to work with to counter disinformation campaigns, they try
to choose people who talk about GESI issues in a positive light. Interview respondents said that
by partnering with these influencers, you are also more likely to reach women and marginalized
groups because they are more likely to watch content that is respectful toward them.
Interview respondents also noted that in their social media listening activities, they frequently
find disinformation campaigns targeted directly at women. For example, the Chinese

198

GS-10F-0033M / 7200AA18M00016, Tasking N088
Communist Party tries to appeal to Muslim women in Indonesia by presenting "pro-Uighur"
messages, in which they dress ethnic Chinese women as native Uighurs and share photos of
them "living their best life."
Interview respondents also noted that in their research, they aim to get a representative sample
of the country, ensuring that women and minorities are included.
MERL APPROACHES
AML is an excellent example of how IIR/MDM activities can conduct rigorous impact
evaluations, while also remaining agile and frequently adapting their approach. The program
runs in three-month sprints: first, adapting existing media literacy content to meet the needs of
Indonesian internet users, then running the media literacy campaigns, testing the effectiveness,
and restarting the cycle by adapting the content again based on the evaluation results. This
allows them to get high-quality information about the effectiveness of their media literacy efforts
and iterate to continuously improve their content. In addition to improving the media literacy
content, the program has improved their evaluation methods over time. They have conducted
focus groups, conducted pre- and post-tests with users (treatment group) and non-users
(control group), and conducted a randomized control trial comparing changes in media literacy
between those who play five minutes of Gali Fakta (the media literacy game) vs. those who play
five minutes of Tetris.
In addition to these frequent evaluations, the program has 16 indicators, including a good mix of
output and outcome indicators. They complement the RCTs, which measure effectiveness of
the messages, by measuring engagement rates to determine whether the content is engaging.
They also rigorously evaluate the technical aspects of the MEWS to ensure that their social
media listening efforts are collecting accurate data.
EVIDENCE OF EFFECTIVENESS
AML appears to be very effective at both identifying social media disinformation campaigns and
improving media literacy among website and game users. Furthermore, the MEWS, the media
literacy game and website, and the media literacy campaigns are all being continually improved
through repeated evaluation and program adaptation.
Early findings from focus group discussions with users of the website and game found that
people were satisfied with the content, finding the lessons to be easy to learn through the
courses and games. People also reported that the user interface was attractive and user
friendly. Most importantly, users reported that they gained useful information on how to
distinguish hoaxes from non-hoaxes and that they believed the website provided a benefit to the
community.
When AML conducted its first between groups (users vs. non-users) pre-/post-test, they found
that the users were 16% more likely than non-users to identify a misinformation headline as
either very or somewhat inaccurate (significant at 90% confidence). After tweaking the media
literacy content, they ran another between groups pre-/post-test and found that there was no

A5. NICARAGUA
CONTEXT
Nicaragua has instituted serious restrictions on freedom of expression and the press in recent
years following a massive wave of citizen protests in 2018.41 The government uses repressive
policies to curb protest and social discontent. In response to the worsening environment, USAID
extended and expanded the budgets of two activities, the Media Strengthening Program and
Voices for All, both of which are nearing the end of their maximum ten-year period. These
programs are designed to complement each other and strengthen the overall media ecosystem.
Part of their programming includes subgrants and rapid response funding to cover the operating
costs of outlets that have struggled to survive as they go into exile and transition to digital
formats.
In late 2020 and early 2021, the government passed a series of laws that increased restrictions
on freedom of expression and freedom of the press, including the Foreign Agents Law and the
Cybercrime Law. These laws sanctioned the media, content producers, and individuals who
disseminate information the government does not like through various channels, including social
media. In recent years, independent media outlets have faced attacks, surveillance, threats, and
closure. Owing to the repressive political environment in Nicaragua, many journalists involved in
USAID-funded programs work from exile. The media sector has also witnessed the accelerated
concentration in the ownership of conventional communication media in the hands of an
economic group close to the ruling Ortega-Murillo family. As a result, there are serious
restrictions on the information available to the public. The government uses its control over the
media to distribute misinformation and disinformation to the Nicaraguan public.
When asked about the unique challenges of working in a rapidly closing political context, USAID
staff said that common approaches like fact-checking are very difficult in Nicaragua. Necessary
predicates like a large pool of professionally trained, independent journalists are much less
common. The relatively low level of capacity requires starting with basic professionalism and
sustainability before more specific approaches can be fully pursued. Threats to journalists
continue to escalate, with the regime now targeting the family members of journalists in exile.

The Voices for All (VFA) project provides critical support for independent media outlets trying to
survive and make credible information available to the public. The project implicitly assumes
that increasing information integrity and societal resilience will help Nicaraguans navigate the
current period of authoritarian backsliding and counter government disinformation. KIl
respondents link program activities to broader efforts to combat disinformation, noting that the
focus currently is on assisting independent outlets in becoming professional and credible so that
they are trusted information sources that can counter misinformation.
PROGRAM ACTIVITIES
Voices for All focuses on organizational strengthening to help independent outlets survive and
become sustainable businesses. In response to the challenges posed by MDM, the project
provides training in fact-checking and verification to media outlets. Some outlets now have fact-
checking sections on their website, but these efforts have been limited due to resource
constraints and the perception that fact-checking may not enhance readership. Also, because
the government is the main producer of information, having journalists actively counter/fact-
check official sources places journalists at risk. As a result, some journalists do not want to be
involved. Currently, training on fact-checking is geared toward larger outlets that have sufficient
staff. For smaller outlets, some of which have only two or three journalists, the project focuses
on helping them build credibility with their own agenda, not just reacting to what the government
is saying.
GENDER / MARGINALIZED COMMUNITIES
Several project components relate directly to women and marginalized communities. For
example, USAID has supported training journalists to conduct news reporting through a gender
lens, viewing stories in terms of how they may affect women differently and including female
sources. USAID has also supported efforts to increase the number of women in leadership
positions in newsrooms and to expand policies against discrimination in media outlets. USAID's
M&E framework includes indicators that track the number of partner outlets producing content
related to gender issues. Progress on this indicator was sporadic: it rose from 23 percent in
2017 to a high of 72 percent in 2019, then declined to 34 percent in 2022. The program also
tracked the number of journalists trained and supported by gender; between 2020 and 2022, the
program trained significantly more female journalists than male. However, with the information
provided, this review cannot say if those trainings took into account the distinct risks to female
journalists or led to improvements in the safety challenges they face.
MERL APPROACHES
In documents included in this review, the most significant M&E indicators for this activity were
audience reach and revenue generation. Given the project aim of helping media outlets expand,
the Mission and IP were particularly interested in audience reach (along with related measures
of engagement). At present, audience reach is primarily measured for online platforms, since
many outlets are currently disseminating content only through social media and websites.

Likewise, efforts to help outlets become financially viable lead to measuring revenues generated
by monetizing content. IPs also track the survival of media outlets, since many have been
closed in recent years due to government raids, confiscation, and threats. In Klls, respondents
noted that in the past, the project conducted audience research, but that this has become
impossible in the current political climate since survey teams are at risk and members of the
public may be unwilling to speak with them. More recently, USAID and the IP developed the
Vibrant Information Barometer (VIBE) to measure how information is produced and used
through 20 indicators based on expert ratings.
EVIDENCE OF EFFECTIVENESS
USAID staff called the survival of Nicaraguan outlets operating in remarkably difficult
circumstances as "the most important, most impressive thing." All of the partner outlets working
with this project have experienced government attacks in the form of office raids, arrests of staff
and editors, and even seizure of imported newspaper ink. USAID staff were certain that many of
these outlets would not exist today if this program had waited until the 2018 protests to begin
supporting media.
Depending on the year, VFA worked with 18 to 34 independent Nicaraguan media outlets
between 2016 and 2022. In 2017, 85 percent of partner outlets reported an increase in users on
their digital platforms; that number was 100 percent in 2019, the year following the protests and
the beginning of the government crackdown. In 2022, it is still more than half, showing that
online audiences continue to grow.
Turning growing audiences into revenue has been more difficult, perhaps not surprising given
the media climate in Nicaragua. It is unclear how long USAID can remain the primary lifeline for
Nicaraguan media. Evaluations project that most partner outlets will not be sustainable within
the decade. This is why USAID has emphasized business sustainability. However, despite
some limited early success in 2017, after the crackdown none of the partner outlets reported an
increase in revenue from non-USG sources until 2022 when the project exceeded its goal for
this indicator for the first time (13 percent of outlets reported gains, better than the goal of 10
percent). The journey from survival to sustainability is long and mostly uphill.

THEORY OF CHANGE & OBJECTIVES
The Media Strengthening Program (MSP) is designed to raise the quality and excellence of
independent journalists so that they can reach and are trusted by all segments of the
Nicaraguan public. As the IP said in an email interview, "It began with a theory of change, with a
strategy aimed at raising the quality and excellence of independent journalists as an essential
factor in the construction of citizenship and the rule of law. The project strongly contributed to
the transition of independent media from analog to digital, strengthening capabilities in content
production for multiple platforms, expanding content and audiences, and positively increasing
citizens'
perception of independent media's quality, rigor, and ethics." In response to MDM, the
program includes trainings on identifying disinformation and ways to combat it through fact-
based news coverage of important areas of Nicaraguan life.
PROGRAM ACTIVITIES
MSP provides training to Nicaragua's embattled independent media. Many of these trainings
focus on increasing the capacities of journalists to do good journalism, especially in the realm of
security and protection from state reprisals and human rights violations. Through the project,
journalists have been trained to respond to emergencies and attacks. Other trainings seek to
improve newsroom operations, help outlets acclimate to digital journalism, and assist in
developing relationships with new audiences. Regarding MDM, the IP held a two-day fact-
checking workshop for journalists with "Animal Politico," a prominent Mexican digital media
platform that ran a highly publicized fact-checking effort during Mexico's elections. The IP for
this project notes that this training occurred in 2017, before the widespread crackdown, meaning
that by the time of the crisis, there were Nicaraguan media that had been trained to respond to
MDM.
GENDER / MARGINALIZED COMMUNITIES
MSP's work on human rights violations also includes violations of the rights of female
journalists. Despite this, the program has consistently trained and supported more male than
female journalists—twice as many in several years. This is in contrast to VFA, which often
trained a greater number of female journalists than male journalists. Neither program provided
this review with indicators on whether the outcomes of that support affected gender-related
outcomes for recipients MSP also tracks the number of "supported programs dedicated to
vulnerable population[s]," and consistently met or exceeded its objectives in this area.

The IP for this project said that its greatest achievements have been in investigative journalism,

The MSP reported uneven revenue growth among partners year-over-year due to the worsening

increased repression and exile, which is why most spent several months in adaptive and

CONTEXT
The proliferation of hate speech and disinformation (HSD) in Libya is undermining the
development of democratic processes and institutions, perpetuating conflict, and chilling speech
and civic participation. Coordinated efforts for countering HSD are therefore critical to Libya's
peaceful political transition.
In Libya, social platforms abound with disinformation and hate speech. Some of it comes from
political actors, both domestic and foreign, who use hate speech and disinformation as a
weapon. Local news outlets and social media have played a role in hardening social and
political polarization when Libya split under two administrations in a divide that eventually led to
the 2019 war, which attracted foreign military intervention on both sides. Countries intervening
in Libya also utilized disinformation and propaganda on social media and conventional media
outlets for their own ends.
Media outlets - including television, streaming platforms, and newspapers - are often tied to a
political or armed faction. Reporting can be highly politicized, lacking in sound methodology or
investigation, and marked by mis- and disinformation. This has contributed to increasing public
distrust of conventional media and greater reliance on social media, particularly Facebook, for
news. All of this creates an information environment that is saturated with hate speech and mis-
and dis-information.
THEORY OF CHANGE & OBJECTIVES
In Libya, USAID-funded information resilience and integrity programming is part of a larger
project, the Libya Elections and Legislative Strengthening Activity (LELSA) that is implemented
by the CEPPS consortium (NDI, IRI, and IFES) and includes subawards to several domestic
and international organizations. LELSA aims to support Libya's political transformation in the
wake of Muammar Gaddafi's removal from power in 2011 and subsequent conflicts and
instability. LELSA includes three overarching objectives that aim to 1) bolster civic processes, 2)
build democratic institutions, and 3) counter corrosive influences.

THEORY OF CHANGE & OBJECTIVES
The TMCS project aims to strengthen the information environment in Tanzania through the
provision of capacity building and material support to journalists and media organizations, civil
society groups, and other related stakeholders. The overall goal is "to support an open, inclusive
environment in which media and civil society provide accurate and impartial information that
promotes participation, inclusion, and accountability" (from the Call for Proposals). The Theory
of change proposes that this goal will be achieved if four related objectives related to the 1) the
media environment, 2) journalist capacity, 3) community radio station capacity, and 4) civil
society capacity are accomplished.
PROGRAM ACTIVITIES
Internews supported media and civil society development through sub-grants to local media-
support and human rights groups, as well as the International Center for Not-for-Profit Law
(ICNL), a U.S.-based international NGO. It also worked with a core group of 16 community radio
stations and provided small grants to 20 CSOs to implement advocacy campaigns using
traditional and social media. In addition, the project supported over 100 Tanzanian media
outlets and local CSOs with training, mentoring, stipends, and workshops to help them report on
legal reforms, the Covid-19 pandemic, elections, reconciliation, and reform processes, gender-
based violence, youth, disability, and other social inclusion issues.
GENDER / MARGINALIZED COMMUNITIES
While none of the project's core objectives relate primarily to gender or marginalized
communities, the TOC does anticipate that the project will lead to better representation of the
"voices of all citizens, including women and youth" in media reporting. The final evaluation
(November 2022) notes that "in terms of Gender and Social Inclusion (GESI)...there have been
consistent efforts by Internews and almost all partners to ensure it is integrated into the project
activities and grants, with significant achievements recorded." A final evaluation of the project
noted several key contributions. First, the project prioritized the inclusion of women in journalist
trainings, leading to positive increases in professionalization and promotion within media outlets.
Second, the project encouraged greater coverage of issues that affect marginalized groups,
including women, the disabled, and others. The final evaluation observed a significant increase
in reporting of relevant issues, including gender-based violence, female genital mutilation, and
the perspectives of disabled citizens. Third, by raising awareness about sexual harassment, the
project has improved the working environment for female journalists within media outlets.
MERL APPROACHES
The MERL approach for this activity included two core components: 1) routine monitoring of
output and outcome indicators by the IP, and 2) evaluations conducted by independent
evaluators.

understand or define those terms?

1. Executive Summary
Overview
Increasing the supply of high-quality information from independent, credible sources and
building societal resilience to mis-, dis-, and mal-information (MDM) is a global priority. In
response, USAID and its Implementing Partners (IPs) have developed and implemented a wide
range of activities designed to mitigate the harms associated with manipulated information
across global regions and sectors, including but not limited to Democracy, Human Rights, and
Governance (DRG), Health, and the Office of Transitional Initiatives (OTI).
This Program Review provides an overview of the breadth and depth of USAID's programming
related to Information Resilience and Integrity (IRI). It is based on a detailed examination of 23
projects that cover all regions where USAID operates and a wide range of activity types,
including "supply-side" interventions focusing on media development, regulatory reform, content
creation, and others - along with "demand-side" interventions that aim to help citizens detect
and critically respond to non-credible information sources, attenuate the influence of content
from malign actors, and achieve related goals.
This Program Review is not an evaluation of USAID's IRI portfolio. Rather, it aims to understand
the types of interventions being funded by USAID; identify gaps in programming; provide an
updated typology that reflects the scope of USAID's IRI programing; examine strategies for
monitoring, evaluations, learning, and research (MERL); and provide a summary of the
emerging evidence on what's working. Based on the findings, the Program Review offers a set
of recommendations to USAID related to programming and MERL strategies. A full description
of the goals and research questions is provided below.
This review draws on two principal information sources. First, the research team carried out a
document review for 23 programs, based on project descriptions, quarterly and annual reports,
M&E plans, evaluations, and other relevant materials provided by USAID and IPs. Second, the
team conducted 20 Key Informant Interviews (Klls) with 41 individuals, including USAID HQ and
Mission personnel, as well as IP staff based in the US and in country offices. In collaboration
with USAID, the study team selected seven countries for in-depth case studies, reflecting the
diversity of contexts and project types that fall under USAID's information resilience and integrity
portfolio. In each case study country, the research team interviewed Mission personnel and in-
country staff from implementing partners.'
Key Findings
1. USAID programming related to information resilience and integrity includes a diverse
set of projects with distinct objectives and theories of change. While the wide set of
activities are all conceptually related, respondents consulted for this report noted some
1 As noted below, the research team was not able to arrange interviews for one of the selected case study
countries, Tanzania.
7

important distinctions in how they understand core objectives. Specifically, some
respondents conceptualize interventions as promoting information integrity and building a
resilient media environment, while others view their efforts as designed to counter MDM,
often related to context-specific threats and actors. While these differences may in part
reflect the lack of agreement on shared terminology, they have
Names of 23 programs reviewed -
alternative frames inform how program designers and implemer
list here.
change and articulate the associated harms they aim to mitigate
varied on whether IRI projects should aim to produce
behavior changes. While some projects, particularly those
related to media literacy and alternative narratives, explicitly
aimed to change individual attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors,
many other projects, especially related to media
development, framed their goals in terms of contributing to
overall information ecosystems.
2. While USAID supports many IRI activities, programming
is concentrated in two main areas: media development
and citizen engagement / literacy. A smaller set of
programs focus on connecting and augmenting the work of
other stakeholders, on monitoring and understanding MDM,
and on responding to MDM through strategic
communications offering alternative narratives.
3. While there is widespread support for addressing cross-cutting issues related to
gender and marginalized / vulnerable groups, few projects make this a central goal,
and respondents disagreed about whether targeted programming was always needed.
Respondents expressed support for the general idea that USAID and IPs should do more to
address MDM related to gender and marginalized groups, which can increase the risks of
violence against these groups and discourage participation in politics, among other harms.
Respondents agreed that these issues were often not being adequately considered during
program design. Consistent with this, the program review found that only eight of 23
projects incorporated cross-cutting issues in meaningful ways. However, views on the
importance of program targeting differed among respondents. While many expressed
support for activities designed to address group-specific harms related to MDM, other
respondents viewed interventions as taking a "whole-of-society" approach that benefited all
social segments, making targeting unnecessary.
4. Theories of change are typically not assessed by existing MERL approaches. The
theories of change articulated in project documents typically emphasize high-level impacts,
including increased availability of quality information, greater demand for impartial
information, increased citizen participation, improved inclusion and tolerance, and greater
transparency and accountability in government. MERL plans, on the other hand, tend to
focus mainly on outputs and short-term outcomes, including the number of journalists
trained and workshops held,the number of legal reforms attempted, the reach of content
8

produced by USAID-supported actors, and other related measures. The focus on outputs
and short-term outcomes reflects the inherent difficulties of measuring long-term outcomes
and impacts for most IRI projects. Moreover, in some cases it is neither desirable nor
feasible to focus on impacts, including in conflict-affected and transitioning countries, where
evolving political condition and project objectives may limit opportunities for measuring
impacts. In other cases, though, opportunities exist for integrating MERL approaches that
have the potential to narrow the gap between the goals expressed in TOCs and the data
collected to track program implementation and effectiveness.
5. There is an insufficient evidence base to allow for definitive conclusions about the
effectiveness of some IRI activities on higher-order outcomes. Impact evaluations
based on randomized-controlled trials and other credible research designs are rare for IRI
projects, and the existing academic literature is under-developed in this area. Despite this,
there is widespread agreement that some interventions - particularly those related to media
development and media literacy - can be effective at building the capacity of media
organizations and other stakeholders to provide accurate, independent information and
building skills citizens need to navigate complex information landscapes. Additional research
will be valuable for helping USAID and IPs more fully "tell the story" of program successes,
test intervention strategies, and examine the relative effectiveness of alternative
approaches.
Summary of Recommendations
Based on the key findings outlined here, as well as others described in subsequent sections, we
offer a set of recommendations related to programming and MERL approaches to USAID and
its partners. The recommendations are described in more detail at the end of the report.
Programmatic Recommendations
1. Expand programming informed by behavior change theory and designed for
adaptability, iteration, and learning.
2. Prioritize refining and expanding media literacy programs.
3. Consider expanding strategic communications programs related to information
resilience.
4. Consider ways of integrating non-media programming more fully in the information
resilience and counter-MDM toolkit.
5. Develop theories of change that match project timelines.
6. Reconsider how USAID approaches relationships with social media platforms in its
programming.
7. Encourage IPs to design programs with deeper consideration of gender equity and
social inclusion (GESI) issues
9

MERL Recommendations
1. USAID should dedicate more resources to MERL for IRI/MDM programs.
2. Programs should consider increased usage of complexity-aware MERL strategies.
3. USAID and IPs should track how programs affect women and people from
marginalized groups as part of routine project monitoring.
4. National opinion surveys are useful for tracking attitudes and behaviors but in most
cases should not be used for outcome indicators.
5. Content reach is not a strong outcome indicator and should be coupled with other
means of assessing audience impact, when possible.
6. USAID should increase the use of impact evaluation methods for some types of
projects.
2. Goals, Research Questions, and Methodology
Goals and Research Questions
The goal of this program review is to examine the portfolio of USAID-funded projects related to
information resilience and integrity. This review does not serve as an evaluation of USAID-
funded projects; rather, it aims to take stock of USAID programming, and examine theories of
change, approaches to cross-cutting issues, monitoring and evaluation strategies, and evidence
of effectiveness. The review is guided by a set of research questions (RQs) initially presented in
the Concept Note and subsequently refined with input from USAID after project launch:
(RQ1) Theories of Change. How do USAID projects define information resilience and
integrity and conceptualize the harms associated with MDM? What types of theories of

Methodology
Document review. The study team compiled and examined program documents provided by
USAID related to 23 projects, including several that are regional in scope (see Annex D for a
list). Documents included: (1) program work plans; (2) quarterly and annual reports; (3) MERL
plans; and (4) and evaluation/research reports (see Annex H for a complete list of documents).
Based on this material, the team catalogued activities by type, refined the typology of USAID
information resilience and integrity programming, and analyzed information related to the core
research questions, focusing on theories of change, MERL strategies, cross-cutting issues, and
evidence of impact.
Key Informant Interviews (Klls). The study team conducted 20 Klls with a total of 41
participants. This included interviews with headquarters personnel from USAID and
Implementing Partners. The team also conducted interviews with USAID Mission staff and IPs in
six case study countries: Ukraine, Georgia, Serbia, Libya, Nicaragua, and Indonesia.? The Klls
for the case studies were designed to complement information obtained through the document
review and allow for further exploration of core topics. The set of case study countries was
chosen in collaboration with USAID to ensure the inclusion of multiple project types and
implementing partners, and to cover multiple regions and political regime types. The study team
conducted all Klls remotely between May 12 and July 14, 2023.

3. Theories of Change
RQ1.1: How do USAID projects define information resilience and integrity and
conceptualize the harms associated with MDM?
Primary Findings:
• USAID staff largely pull from similar definitions of MDM and consider information
resilience a broader, longer-term goal than countering MDM.
• The harms attributed to MDM and low information resilience are many and varied,
producing several distinct families of change theories.
RQ1.2: What types of theories ofchange (TOC) arebeing used by projects seeking to
prevent or address these harms?
Primary Finding:
•
While USAID supports many IRI activities, programming is concentrated in two main
areas: media development and citizen engagement / literacy. Strict "counter-MDM"
activities are rare.
RQ1.3: Are there ways to improve TOCs for USAID's activities?
Primary Finding:
•
Theories of change shouldbe less abstract and more measurable, better connecting
proposed activities to desired changes, which were often high-level and vague.
Improving information resilience, promoting information integrity, and responding to MDM are
broad goals. The projects considered in this review tackled them in many different ways: some
attempt to improve the supply of quality media and public access to it. Others try to understand
and respond directly to low-integrity information from bad actors. Still others disseminate
alternative narratives meant to blunt the impact of MDM and promote social cohesion and other
goals.
This section of the report explores how programs describe what they aim to achieve, and how
they hope to achieve it. It explores competing conceptions of the core problem, examines the
types of harms programs are concerned with, and summarizes common interventions used to
prevent or mitigate those harms. Some theories of change operate purely on a systemic level
such as national media environments, while others are focused on specific changes in
behaviors or (more rarely) attitudes.
Not every program provided documents explicitly laying out a theory of change, and even fewer
used the classic "if-then," format. For those projects that did not, this review tries to infer one
from stated objectives or other available information. Sometimes, interviews were the best way
12

of assessing a given program's theory of change. Most projects focused on media development,
support for journalists and media outlets, or various forms of media literacy. Other theories of
change were less well-represented.
In general, even theories of change that were explicitly spelled out in program documents
sometimes contained gaps, leaps of logic, or vagaries that inhibit monitoring and evaluation.
This often leads to disconnects between theories of change and MERL indicators. These issues
are elaborated on in later sections that take stock of activities and MERL approaches.
Defining the Problem
The goals of promoting high-integrity information and a resilient media environment are distinct
from countering MDM. This distinction was an important theme during interviews. Which of
these frames a program uses often informs its theory of changeas does the way it articulates
the associated harms.
The Executive Branchhas already weighed in on this distinction and provided a starting point
for common definitions of a wider frame. In a December 2022 "Roadmap for Researchers on
Priorities Related to Information Integrity Research and Development,"the National Science &
Technology Council laid out four goals:3
- to help individuals discern between "high-integrity" and "low-integrity" information,
- to prevent or minimize avoidable harms from information manipulation,
- to promote resiliencethe ability of people to operate in the context of potentially
questionable information and of communities to "maintain appropriate levels of
information integrity" despite uncertainty or active manipulations,
- and the collection of "high-quality evidence" for evaluating strategies for addressing
information integrity challenges.
This suggests that at high levels within the US government, a distinction is being made between
two terms that were often used but not well-defined during interviews for this project:

The goals of promoting high-integrity information and a resilient media environment are distinct
from countering MDM (or "low-integrity information"). This distinction was an important theme
during interviews. Which of these frames a program uses often informs its theory of changeas
does the way it articulates the associated harms.
Many interview participants referenced "Mis-, Dis-, and Mal-information" as challenges to
information integrity and resilience. This specific combination of terms reflects that USAID staff
largely draw on the conceptual framework laid out by Claire Wardle's work on "Information
Disorder." When asked, all of the USAID staff interviewed for this report defined these terms as
Wardle does: misinformation is the incidental, unintentional spread of false or misleading
information—essentially rumors—while disinformation is understood to be intentional. (Mal-
information is used less commonly and refers to true information used intentionally to harm,
such as the release of hacked materials.) Many interviewees referenced Wardle and her work
directly by name.
Some interview participants also felt that the definitions on offer, while widely cited, lacked a
necessary degree of clarity around nuanced and sometimes sensitive issues. Some felt that
"countering MDM" evokes geopolitical aspects of strategic communications by external
authoritarian governments, even in contexts where domestic sources of MDM were more
influential and harmful. Several expressed an appetite for more precise termseven MDM
obscures important differences between mis-and disinformation, for instance.
Interviewees typically agreed that resilience is a longer-term,
broader goal than countering MDM. A few said that countering
MDM was more "reactive" than promoting IRI. Some took a
societal perspective and distinguished between efforts to
expose and hold bad actors accountable and efforts to create
a resilient environment in which those actors are less harmful.
Others took a more individual-level perspective, seeking to
identify and reduce harmful "end-state behaviors" motivated
by MDM.

A smaller number of programs focused on producing attitudinal changes, rather than behavioral
changes. For example, the Georgia Information Integrity Project (GIIP), seeks to promote
solidarity within Georgia and weaken disinformation narratives targeting the anxieties about
Georgia's relationship with Europe and NATO through strategic communications. An example
was the "Fruits of Heroism" campaign it developed in conjunction with Georgian partners for
audiences in rural communities near the contested border with Russia. Individuals associated
with this program said that communities in those areas often feel cut off, neglected by Tbilisi,
and vulnerable to Russian hostility; this campaign recast them as patriotic heroes on the front
line and encouraged Georgians in the capital to consume produce from those regions.
Categorizing Theories of Change
This review groups the theories of change pursued by USAID programs into five categories. By
far the two largest are programs aiming to improve citizen engagement with media and those
working to support national media sectors through systemic reform and increased capacity in
individual organizations. A smaller set of programs focus on connecting and augmenting the
work of other stakeholders, on monitoring and understanding MDM and its sources, and on
responding to MDM through strategic communications offering alternative narratives.
1. Citizen engagement with information. Projects in this area tend to center the well-informed
citizen as a necessary component of democracy. These programs often work to provide "neutral
information" to audiences so they can, for example, make informed decisions during elections.
16

They might also seek to mitigate harms like voter suppression through disinformation. Many
programs focus on developing some element of media literacy. Media literacy is understood in
many different ways, and programs under the media literacy umbrella include those aiming to
educate citizens about the media ecosystem, raise awareness of MDM, or help citizens identify
and avoid sharing rumors and propaganda.
Examples of the types of theories of change being used in this area include the following:
• IF critical thinking skills and media information literacy among citizens are
strengthened...THEN citizens will use more accurate, objective news and information in
their decision-making. (Azerbaijan Media and Journalism Activity)
• IF public demand for quality journalism grows...THEN the civically relevant role of media will
be strengthened, and citizens will be equipped with quality information that counters malign
influence and supports European integration. (Media Program in Ukraine)
• IF youth gain and apply media literacy and critical thinking skills as part of their education
and in other youth-friendly formats....and IF they demand and drive increased volume of
high-quality, fact-based, and relevant professional media content, THEN youth will be able
to not only navigate but also shape an information ecosystem that informs and engages as
opposed to divides and polarizes, resulting in increased resilience to disinformation and
efforts to undermine democracy. (North Macedonia, YouThink)
2. Systemic and organizational support to media. Programs sometimes draw an explicit link
between audience demand for high quality content—driven by their ability to recognize and
access it-and the increased supply of that content, driven by audience growth and other forms
of support to both the media sector, individual outlets, and related civil society groups.
Many programs centered their theory of change on this support, which can include training for
journalists, legal and technological support, grants to modernize newsroom business practices,
provision of new infrastructure or equipment, advocacy for legal and regulatory reforms affecting
the enabling environment for media, and support for independent high-quality content, among
other things. Interviewed individuals were quick to point out that much of this is "traditional
media activity" supported by USAID, which can be effective for reason beyond contributing to
IRI. For example, some projects mentioned the watchdog role of media, while others
emphasized that only professional, credible media can establish the bonds of trust with
audiences necessary to inform the public. Some stressed that to survive and reach their full
potential, media needs to make significant improvements to its business operations.
Example TOCs in this area include:
• The purpose of [this program] was to increase media independence and create a more
competitive and self-sustaining media environment [so that] citizens can be informed and
hold their government accountable. To achieve its purpose, the Activity had two
intermediate objectives: to support the development of a more enabling legal, regulatory,

and market environment for media, and to support the development of financial
sustainability, innovation, and partnerships in the media sector. (Serbia, Strengthening
Media Systems)
• If the legal and regulatory environment for media is strengthened, targeted media outlets
become more independent and professional, and access to high quality public interest
reporting increases, the media sector will be more vibrant, independent, and capable of
shaping democratic discourse. (Democratic Republic of the Congo, Media Sector
Development Activity)
• IF the media enabling environment...is improved and legal restrictions on the press and
freedom of expression are reduced while journalist safety is promoted; and IF the skills and
capacity of national media outlets, community radio stations, and journalists including
women and youth is strengthened...THEN media and civil society will be better able to
provide accurate and impartial information that represents the voices of all citizens, including
women and youth, and enables citizens to engage in democratic processes. (Tanzania, the
Boresha Habari Project)
3. Networks and hubs focused on the information environment. Some programs aimed to
increase capacity of local partners through hubs dedicated to research, training, and co-creation
of projects and campaigns:
• The network is founded on the idea that regional hubs are the drivers of change and
creators of innovations that address their civic space challenges. Over the years, the
resources, innovation processes, research, workshops, and campaigns developed and used
by each regional hub have flowed across the network and spread from one regional hub to
another. (Civil Society Innovation Initiative)
4. Research and media monitoring. Other projects focused on understanding narratives within
the media environment and how they spread. Interviewees conveyed that this was crucial for
designing better interventions that effectively target context-specific sources of MDM,
particularly in countries where assumptions about the sources of MDM and their influence have
not been rigorously tested. But no project was primarily or solely devoted to researching,
monitoring, or exposing MDM.
Hub projects like GIIP in Georgia often included a research component. In fact, the GIIP was
one of the few to mention a research tool in its theory of change, shown below.
5. Strategic communications. The GIIP was also one of the few programs with a theory of
change in the final category: the use of strategic communications to offer alternatives to
disinformation narratives. Its full theory of change reads:
• IF the USAID GIIP is able to map the actors, vectors, channels and audiences within the
disinformation ecosystem in Georgia; AND IF: the project can bring together a diverse
network of private and public sector actors across Georgia, building their capacity to work
collectively to develop and test responses to disinformation identified through the ecosystem
18

map, THEN: Network Partners can develop evidence-based, effective, scalable initiatives to
counter disinformation in Georgia, sharing learnings throughout the network; AND IF:
stakeholders can understand the impact of scalable solutions on target audiences, enabling
the identification of sustainable responses to disinformation, and using learnings to drive
advocacy for policy change at government level; THEN: vulnerable audiences in Georgia
will develop and awareness of and response to disinformation, increasing societal resilience
to misinformation and malign influence. (Georgia Information Integrity Project)
As in the previous example of GIIP's "Fruits of Heroism" campaign, these alternative narratives
were not intended to debunk disinformation or correct false claims. Rather, they can be seen as
serving both a supply and a demand function: they supply narratives that reframe social issues
for audiences in ways that lower the demand for and the effectiveness of MDM.

4. Stocktaking of Activities
This section takes stock of USAID's information resilience and integrity programming, identifying
common approaches, relating programs to theories of change, and noting gaps in programming.
It also provides an updated typology of USAID-funded programs designed to assist USAID in
20

communicating what the agency is currently fundings in a concise, visual format for a variety of
audiences, including Mission personnel and others interested in exploring potential intervention
strategies.
Analysis of the theories of change described above revealed five major programming
categories, represented in the revised typology shown in Figure 1. To examine how USAID-
funded programs relate to this typology, the research team counted how many projects include
components related to each of the five categories and sub-categories (see Figure 2). As noted
above, the most well-represented category is systemic and organizational support for media,
which captures various supply-side measures for improving IRI. The second most well-
represented is improving citizen engagement with mediawhich includes methods for
promoting IRI by increasing audience demand for high-integrity content and reducing demand
for its opposite. Less well-represented were other categories focused on understanding and
mitigating harms from low-integrity information (either on the supply or demand side).
Based on the revised typology, this section also examines common MERL indicators, grouping
them by output indicators (representing activities) and outcome indicators (representing
progress toward objectives). In most cases, it is difficult to ascribe any causal relationship
between outputs and outcomes, or to say whether outcomes promote desired macro-level
changes. For example, a participant can attend a training, but not apply the skills learned; if they
do apply those skills, they still might not see the benefits the training was supposed to promote.
A Proposed Typology for USAID Programs Included in This Review
As a first step, NORC reviewed the initial typology developed by USAID staff to categorize
programs." This typology captured most of the programs included in this review but was
somewhat cumbersome. The nine categories had significant overlap—for example, "legal and
regulatory" was included both its own category and as a form of support under media
development. An important caveat is that the revised typology is based only on the 23 programs
included in this review and does not reflect other activity types that USAID may support for
which program materials were unavailable or could not be shared with the review team.
Many USAID programs are large with many components, and so may be placed in more than
one category. Given the broad scope of many programs, it is probably not feasibleor even
helpful—to create a typology in which each program fits into only one category. However, it is
possible to reduce the number of categories overall, making the typology easier to use and
interpret. The revised condenses the nine categories included in the initial typology into five
based on the similarity of their approaches and objectives.
Programs are organized across two axes in the typology. First, column labels on the top of the
typology show how the five categories relate to core goals related to (1) information resilience
(programs improving media production and consumption) and (2) harm mitigation/information
