Domestic and Transnational Authoritarianism
Reading List
(All sources in purple are cross-listed sources)
(Note: sources highlighted in yellow are updates by Aqil Shah)
The Resurgence of Authoritarianism: The Problem
Evidence and Documentation of the Rise of Authoritarianism:
• V-Dem 2022 Report: Autocratization Changing Nature?, March 2022
The annual report from the Varieties of Democracy, a Swedish-based international
institute focused on methodologically rigorous research on democracy and autocracy
continues the previous documentation of the global decline of democracy. In addition, it
highlights 3 developments: increasing number of coups (5 in 2021), the large wave of
polarization and how it correlates with increases in autocratization, and how
mis/disinformation by governments is multiplying. They also point out the official
statistics from autocracies are not reliable, which raises concerns for policy-making
across sectors.
• V-Dem 2021 Report: Autocratization Turns Viral, March 2021
Annual report from the Varieties of Democracy, that documents the accelerating global
decline of democracy, the rise of authoritarianism, and the impact of the Covid-19
pandemic. Across different contexts autocratization follows a similar pattern of 1)
restrictions on the media; 2) delegitimization of opponents; 3) disinformation campaigns;
4) attack on democratic institutions. Great infographics.
• V-Dem 2020 Democracy Report: Autocratization Surges, Resistance Grows
Discusses the rise of autocracy, but also how in 2019 there were many pro-democracy
protests movements in a diverse set of countries. Highlights the declining quality of
elections in multiple countries. Points how for the first time since 2001 the majority of
countries are autocracies.
• Freedom House 2021 Freedom in the World Report: Democracy Under Siege, 2021
Documents the global decline of democracy and the rise of authoritarianism, including in
the United States and by region. Discusses the influence of the Covid-19 on democracy
and authoritarianism. Emphasizes the growing antidemocratic influence of the PRC.
Uses a different methodology than V-Dem but comes to similar conclusions. Great
infographics.
3

• BTI 2020, Resistance to Democratic Regression and Authoritarian Rule is Growing,
2020
Analysis from the German Bertelsmann Stiftung Transformation Index (BTI) on political
transformations during the 2017-2019 period. Similar to V-Dem, the report is based on
the results from surveys of 100s of regional experts. Based on extensive data, the report
makes 3 major conclusions: 1) democracies face increasing domestic challenges; 2)
autocracies have adopted new, effective survival strategies; 3) the rise of China and
increased assertiveness of Russia has supported the spread of autocracy. In addition,
the report argues that there is less citizen support for democracy, elite corruption is a
widespread source of dissatisfaction, and political parties have become weak.
• General Resource Podcast, NED Authoritarianism--POWER 3.0
Regular podcast by the American National Endowment for Democracy (NED) about the
authoritarian resurgence and examples of democratic resilience, including topics such as
the PRC government's BRI, digital authoritarianism, disinformation, and corruption.
Features different expert guests.
• NED, Sharp Power: Rising Authoritarian Influence in the Democratic World, 2017
Defines authoritarian "sharp power," as power that "pierces, penetrates, or perforates the
political and information environments in the targeted countries." Unlike BTI and V-Dem
reports this paper focuses more on the promotion of authoritarianism and through
examining 4 cases-- Argentina, Peru, Poland, and Slovakia—investigates Russia and
China's sharp power. Argues for 5 policy responses: 1) address the shortage of
information about China and Russia in recipient countries; 2) unmask often secretive
authoritarian influence; 3) build democratic resilience; 4) reaffirm support for democratic
values; 5) reconceptualize "soft power" as the more threatening "sharp power."
• Journal of Democracy, Authoritarian Vestiges in Fledgling Democracies, 2021
Argues that there are 3 main forms of authoritarian vestiges in new democracies:
authoritarian successor parties, authoritarian-era constitutions, and subnational
authoritarian enclaves. Authoritarian successor parties and constitutions have mixed
effects on democracy; subnational authoritarianism is always a problem. For example,
authoritarian successor parties can help develop stable interparty competition and
ensure that supporters participate in the new democratic system.
• Anna Luhrmann and Staffan Lindberg. "A Third Wave of Autocratization is Here: What is
New about it?" Democratization 26, no. 7 (2019): 1095-1113.
This widely cited article by Luhrman and Lindberg uses V-Dem data (episodes of
democratic regression from 1900 to 2017) to demonstrate the unfolding of what they
describe as a "third wave of "autocratization." Autocratization is an umbrella concept that
encompasses three distinct processes: (a) decline in the core institutions of a democratic
regime ("democratic recession"), (b) the collapse of democracy ("democratic
4

breakdown"); and (c) the degradation of democratic qualities in authoritarian regimes
("autocratic consolidation"). While the authors agree with the prevailing wisdom in the
literature that "autocratization" gradually erodes democratic institutions from behind a
legal-democratic facade, they caution against widespread democratic pessimism by
showing that the current level of democratic regression is relatively modest compared to
previous waves of autocratization, and the global share of democratic countries has
remained stable.
• Bermeo, Nancy. "On Democratic Backsliding." Journal of Democracy 27 (2016): 5-19
In this influential and much cited paper, Bermeo argues that the current trend of
democratic backsliding (defined as the state-led debilitation or elimination of any of the
political institutions that sustain an existing democracy) is qualitatively different from the
the previous trend of authoritarian regression marked by classic military coups,
autocratic executive takeovers (autogolpe) and blatant election rigging. Instead,
backsliding occurs in three ways: (1) "promissory coups" (the ouster of an elected
government with the promise of a swift restoration of democracy), (2) the expansion of
executive power, and the erosion of horizontal checks-and-balances, and (3) the
strategic manipulation of elections. However, Bermeo concludes on an optimistic note:
the current wave of democratic backsliding may be more easily reversed than the past,
and democratic breakdowns often lead to dictatorships that are short-lived and "less
authoritarian."
• Ginsburg, Tom, and Aziz Z. Huq. "Democracy's 'Near Misses'." Journal of Democracy 29
(2018): 16-30.
The authors highlight the temporal differences between old and new forms of
autocratization, emphasizing that the current predominant form is not the "sudden
reversal", but a slow and incremental process in which democratically elected leaders
gradually undercut the institutional and normative features of democracy.
• Larry Diamond (2021) Democratic regression in comparative perspective: scope,
methods, and causes, Democratization, 28:1, 22-42
In this article, Larry Diamond provides a comparative snapshot of the global wave of
democratic regression that began in the early 200s and has since deepened and
endured. Using Freedom House democracy scores, Diamond documents three major
backsliding trends over the past 14 years: (1) a steady decline in the average levels of
democratic freedom/quality in most parts of the world, (2) an accelerated pace of
democratic breakdowns and (3), a decline in the number of democratic transitions
especially in the past five years. Moreover, Diamond finds that democratic decline has
particularly affected the G-20 countries and other populous and geopolitically strategic
countries. The author confirms the general pattern of democratic decline observed by
other scholars: incremental degradation of democracy at the hands of populist elected
5

leaders who erode institutional checks, neutralize the political opposition, and curtail
independent media and dissenting voices in civil society. The principal domestic cause of
this worldwide process of democratic backsliding, according to Diamond, is weak and
declining rule of law. But international factors have also been instrumental, generating
economic and social strains that lower the constraints and risks autocrats face when
they strangulate democracy.
• Ding Iza, and Slater, Dan. "Democratic Decoupling." Democratization 28 (2021).
Ding and Slater show that many democratic declines lead to "democratic decoupling,"
whereby a "systematic gap" opens up between the constitutive features of liberal
democracy: electoral competition remains robust but civil and political rights diminish. In
this process, "Iliberal juggernauts" such as Narendra Modi in India, Thailand's Thaksin
Shinawatra and Rodrigo Duterte in the Philippines assume power through relatively free
elections but use autocratic tactics to erode/damage democratic institutions and rights.
• Larry Diamond, "A World Without American Democracy? The Global Consequences of
the United States' Democratic Backsliding," Foreign Affairs July 2021.
Diamond argues that the failure of US democracy would have dire consequences for
global democracy because it would encourage the spread of antidemocratic norms.
• Diamond, L. J., Plattner, M. F., & Walker, C. (Eds.). (2016). Authoritarianism goes global:
The challenge to democracy. Johns Hopkins University Press.
United States and India have experienced a decline of democratic values and norms.
This edited volume contends that authoritarianism has gone global because a)
authoritarian countries have been more assertive and have shared authoritarian tactics
and practices with each other and b) in doing so, they have challenged the liberal
international political order and standing of liberal democracy. The authors focus on
"soft-power" competition centering on the role of information/disinformation war, civil
society, and democratic norms.
• IDEA, Global State of Democracy Report 2021
The report documents how during the COVID-19 pandemic the number of democracies
has declined and there has been increased autocratization. Includes their plan for
democratic renewal.
• Pew Research Center, "The World's Democracies: How satisfied is the citizenry?"
December 2021
Recent research from Pew in 17 of the world's democracies found four major themes. 1)
Many say democracy is not delivering for them and want political reform. 2) Democracy
is a popular idea, but commitment to democratic principles is not always strong. 3)
Political and social divisions are amplifying the challenges of democracy. 4) People see
6

political elites as out of touch—and they want a stronger voice in politics and
policy-making. Discussion with Polly Mackenzie, Demos Chief Executive (UK) and
Seema Shah, International IDEA Head of Democracy Assessment about possible
causes of why. (Notes)
Cooley, A. (2015). Authoritarianism Goes Global: Countering Democratic Norms. Journal
of Democracy 26(3).
This article demonstrates the transformation of authoritarianism and the rising influence
of non-Western powers and norms over the past decade. It explains how authoritarians
implement the novel apparatus as well as practices, institutions, and alternative values to
their advantage against the liberal international order. Cooley argues that global political
changes and systemic transformations resulted in alternative norms that challenge
liberal democracy and prioritize state security, civilizational diversity, and traditional
norms. The author demonstrates these changes via a special emphasis on
nongovernmental organizations (NGOs).
• Anne Applebaum, "The Bad Guys Are Winning" The Atlantic November 15, 2021
Applebaum begins the article with a discussion of the situation in Belarus and opposition
leader Tsikhanouskaya. She discusses how autocracy today is different and is defined
by "sophisticated networks composed of kleptocratic financial structures, security
services (military, police, paramilitary groups, surveillance), and professional
propagandists. The members of these networks are connected not only within a given
country, but among many countries. The corrupt, state-controlled companies in one
dictatorship do business with corrupt, state-controlled companies in another." Applebaum
also argues that autocrats today are impervious to international criticism and are able to
act with impunity.
• Erica Chenoweth and Zoe Marks, "Revenge of the Patriarchs: Why Autocrats Fear
Women." Foreign Affairs March/April 2022
The authors argue that the current resurgence of authoritarianism often includes an
attack on women's rights. Referencing cases such as Brazil, Hungary, and Poland they
talk about how illiberal leaders use "traditional gender roles" arguments to attack
"Western" ideas about human rights and democracy and gain political support.
"Established autocrats and right-wing nationalist leaders in contested democracies are
united in their use of hierarchical gender relations to shore up nationalist, top-down,
male-dominated rule. Having long fought against social hierarchies that consolidate
power in the hands of the few, feminist movements are a powerful weapon against
authoritarianism."
• Fareed Zakaria, "Rise of Illiberal Democracy." Foreign Affairs Nov/Dec 1997
A highly influential article where Zakaria raises the importance of thinking about
democracy beyond elections and the key role of what he calls constitutional liberalism:
7

"rule of law, a separation of powers, and the protection of basic liberties of speech,
assembly, religion, and property." States where there are elections, but not constitutional
liberalism, are illiberal democracies, and Zakaria argued 25 years ago that we were
witnessing the spread of these types of regimes.
• IRI, Freedom at Risk: The Challenge of the Century, A Global Survey on Democracy in
55 Countries, 2022.
• Book--Anne Applebaum, Twilight of Democracy: The Seductive Lure of Authoritarianism,
2020
Applebaum discusses the erosion of democracy in Poland, Hungary, and the United
States, with a focus on the postcommunist historical experience. Also, it connects Brexit
and Catalan independence movement to the decline of democracy. She intersects the
analysis with her personal experiences (her husband is a well-known Polish politician).
Focuses on the allure of nostalgia and nationalism combined with disinformation to
explain why people support nondemocratic leaders.
• Book--Madeline Albright, Fascism: A Warning, 2018.
Based on her personal experience and analysis of interwar Europe, Albright argues that
fascism is not restricted to history, but is again a threat to peace and stability in the 21st
century. The tactics of leaders, such as Turkey's Erdoğan, Venezuela's Maduro,
Hungary's Orbán, replicate that of Mussolini and Hitler. She also raised concerns about
President Trump's attacks on democratic norms. Offers policy suggestions for how the
US should respond.
• Book--Krastev and Holmes, The Light That Failed: Why the West is Losing the Fight for
Democracy, 2019
Krastev and Holmes focus on the erosion of democracy in Central Europe and Russia.
Includes some discussion of the rise of China and the influence of its model. They argue
that the decline of democracy stems from the failure of the postcommunist policy in the
region, especially its emphasis on becoming "Westernized." Argue that the need to
imitate Western liberalism breeds resentment and dissatisfaction. [Falls into the category
of blaming the West for the failure of democracy in Russia].
• Book--Timothy Snyder, On Tyranny: Twenty Lessons from the Twentieth Century 2017
A very short book by a historian that, based on the interwar experience, offers 20 brief
lessons (e.g., contribute to good causes and listen for dangerous words) on how
individuals should act to prevent the rise of tyranny.
• Book--Levitsky, Steven and Daniel Ziblatt. How Democracies Die. New York: Crown,
2018.
8

This book has been widely discussed among academics and has had a major influence
on current academic thinking. Levitsky and Ziblatt, looking at the cases of Chavez,
Mussolini, Hitler, and Trump, argue that today democracies die at the hands of elected
rulers. Institutions are insufficient to protect democracy, you also need democratic
norms, especially mutual toleration and forbearance (politicians using restraint when
exercising their power). Outline a widely used index of authoritarian behavior. Argue that
Chavez, Mussolini, etc. gained power when elites and political parties granted them
legitimacy and failed to adequately assess the threat these outside actors presented to
the system. Also, discuss cases of democratic resilience in interwar Belgium and
Finland.
• Book-Cooper, Luke. Authoritarian Contagion. Interview on PRI's The World:
[link omitted]
• Book—Przeworski, Adam. Crisis of Democracy. Cambridge: Cambridge University
Press, 2019.
Using a mix of methodological approaches (statistical analysis, formal modeling, and
historical case studies), Przeworski points out that democracies that have experienced
multiple peaceful changes of power, are fairly wealthy, and have strong political parties
have generally survived. However, the combination of high levels of inequality, political
polarization and increased political violence are real threats to even consolidated
democracies. Przeworski's research also supports Levitsky and Ziblatt's conclusions
about how democracy canbe slowly and gradually eroded.
• Book—Tomini, Luca. When Democracies Collapse: Assessing Transitions to
Non-democratic Regimes in the Contemporary World, 2018.
Tomini argues that the process of democratic backsliding is distinct from
democratization; in other words, autocratization is not necessarily caused by the
absence of the causal factors that support democracy. Tomini provides a great summary
of the scholarship on democratic regression. Then using a mixed-method approach that
incorporates a sophisticated Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA) and
process-tracing to develop 4 models of transition away from democracy. The 4 models
incorporate structural conditions (economic inequality or lack of economic development
+ ethnolinguistically divided society), proximate conditions (volatility of political party
system, concentration of executive power, and social instability), and decisions/norms of
political elites. Four models: incumbent entrenchment (under conditions of economic
inequality and social division the incumbents fearing demands for more representation
from society erode democracy to maintain power); opposition takeover (conditions of
economic crisis, underrepresentation of parts of society in power the system loses
legitimacy and an opposition movement gains power and then turns undemocratic);
democratic coup (military seizes power claiming they are doing it to "protect democracy"
from the perceived threat from the incumbent); stabilizing coup (military seizes power in
g

the name of stability). Tomini's analysis focuses on the importance of existing structural
conditions and the decisions and normative commitment to democracy of political elites.
Haggard & Kauffman, Backsliding: Democratic Regress in the Contemporary World (Cambridge
University Press, 2021)
Stephan Haggard and Robert Kaufman, two veteran democracy scholars, draw on extensive
case studies (the US, cases from Latin America, Eastern Europe, and Africa) to explain the
causes of democratic backsliding. They identify three interrelated sources of democratic
regression: pernicious polarization; party system realignments/legislative capture, and
incrementalism (the slow dismantling of democratic checks and balances). The book also
examines the international context of backsliding and the role of new technology.
Examples of Specific Pro-Authoritarian Tactics:
• Freedom House, Perspectives on Everyday Transnational Repression in an Age of
Globalization, 2020
Provides examples and analysis of the increase of extraterritorial authoritarian rule,
including using digital tools to surveil anti-regime activists abroad, cyberattacks, online
harassment, etc. Also, highlights "coercion by proxy," where autocratic governments use
threats,attacks, or imprisonment of family members or friends to silence critics abroad.
Calls on host countries to help counter this transnational repression.
• NED, Commanding Ideas: Think Tanks as Platforms for Authoritarian Influence, 2020
Part of NED's sharp power and democratic resilience series of publications that
discusses how authoritarian regimes have adapted "think tanks" to support their
autocracies and as instruments of sharp power abroad. Cautions think tanks in
democratic states about their relationships and interactions with these authoritarian
based think tanks.
Theories about Why People May Support Authoritarianism:
• Stanley Feldman, Authoritarianism, Threat and Intolerance,
Focuses on political philosophical arguments about the inherent tradeoffs in the struggle
to maintain social order and authoritarian support at the individual level. Argues that the
distribution of someone on an authoritarian scale is determined by the relative
importance they place on personal autonomy vs. social conformity. If someone values
personal freedom, then they will only support restrictions on liberties if there is a threat to
safety and security. If someone values social conformity, then they are intolerant towards
perceived threats to traditional values and norms. Uses a 2016 survey of American
voters to test the theory. [Some questionable proxy measures are used in the analysis].
• Global Policy Journal, How Fear and Anger Impact Democracy, 2019
10

Taking a political psychology approach, the author investigates how the emotions of fear
and anger impact democracy. Finds that when people are fearful, they are less
supportive of aggressive, risk-taking actions. In contrast, when they are angry, they are
resistant to contrary information, and have increased support for leaders that present
strength.
Book-Norris, Pipa, and Inglehart, Ronald. Cultural Backlash: Trump, Brexit and
Authoritarian Poplism. Cambridge University Press, 2019.
In this book, two prominent comparative political scientists, offer a distinct 'cultural'
explanation of the rise of authoritarian populism in advanced democracies. Their main
argument: societies move towards more liberal values over time which creates a divide
between older conservative authoritarian cohorts and younger liberal ones. Societies
reach a cultural backlash 'tipping point,' so they contend,' when the older cohorts fear
losing their majority status and turn to populist-authoritarian parties that promise to stem
the tide of liberalism. However, the idea that older-younger cohorts in a society polarize
along consverative-liberal values seems empirically weak/problematic.
Guriev, S., & Treisman, D. (2020). The Popularity of Authoritarian Leaders: A
Cross-National Investigation. World Politics, 72(4), 601-638.
How do citizens in authoritarian states feel about their leaders? While some dictators
rule through terror, others seem genuinely popular. Using the Gallup World Poll's panel
of more than one hundred-forty countries in 2006-2016, the authors show that the
drivers of political approval differ across regime types. Although brutal repression in
overt dictatorships could cause respondents to falsify their preferences, in milder
informational autocracies, greater repression actually predicts lower approval. In
autocracies as in democracies, economic performance matters and citizens' economic
perceptions, while not perfectly accurate, track objective indicators. Dictators also benefit
from greater perceived public safety, but the authors find no such effect in democracies.
Covert censorship of the media and the Internet is associated with higher approval in
autocracies—in particular, in informational ones—but ratings fall when citizens recognize
censorship. In informational autocracies, executive elections trigger a ratings surge if
there is leader turnover, but, unlike in democracies, re-elected autocrats enjoy little
honeymoon.
Owen, C. (2020). Participatory authoritarianism: From bureaucratic transformation to
civic participation in Russia and China. Review of International Studies, 46(4), 415-434.
doi:10.1017/S0260210520000248
This article explores the way in which Russian and Chinese governments have
rearticulated global trends towards active citizenship and participatory governance, and
integrated them into pre-existing illiberal political traditions. The author proposes the
concept of 'participatory authoritarianism' to capture the resulting practices of local
11

governance that, on the one hand, enable citizens to engage directly with local officials
in the policy process, but limit, direct, and control civic participation on the other. The
article explores the emergence of discourses of active citizenship at the national level
and the accompanying legislative development of government-organized participatory
mechanisms, demonstrating how the twin logics of openness and control, pluralism and
monism, are built into their rationale and implementation. It argues that as state
bureaucracies have integrated into international financial markets, so new participatory
mechanisms have become more important for local governance as government
agencies have lost the monopoly of information for effective policymaking. Practices of
participatory authoritarianism enable governments to implement public sector reform
while directing increased civic agency into non-threatening channels.
PRC-specific but with broader implications:
• Lily L. Tsai, Minh Trinh, and Shiyao Liu, "What Makes Anti-corruption Punishment
Popular? Individual-Level Evidence from China." The Journal of Politics, 2022 84:1,
602-606.
How do authoritarian regimes sustain their popularity? More specifically, how do
anti-corruption campaigns affect public support for such regimes? Using an
experimental design to measure the individual preferences of Chinese citizens, the
paper finds that citizens favorably view officials who punish corrupt subordinates
because such actions demonstrate both their competence and moral commitment to the
public's values. Significantly, the paper also shows that citizens' positive views of
anti-corruption outweigh support for other sources of authoritarian support (e.g.,
economic performance, welfare provision), suggesting the instrumental value of
corruption crackdowns for autocrats seeking to bolster their public backing. The study
helps explain how authoritarian regimes generate public support to endure in power
rather than just relying on strategies of repression and social control.
• Cunningham, Edward, Tony Saich, and Jesse Turiel. 2020. "Understanding CCP
Resilience: Surveying Chinese Public Opinion through Time." Technical report, Ash
Center for Democratic Governance and Innovation, Harvard University.
This policy brief uses results from a unique, longitudinal nationally representative survey
of Chinese citizens (starting in 2003) to show that public support for the CCP has
increased over time. Whether evaluating national level policies or the performance of
local officials, citizens rate the CCP as competent and effective. Interestingly, citizens
from the poorer, rural areas of the country are likely to report higher increases in
satisfaction. However, citizens' attitudes appear to be sensitive to concrete changes in
their material well-being (i.e., economic growth, environmental decay). These findings
12

suggest that CCP rule remains resilient but public support hinges on its ability to
continue to provide high living standards.
• Teets, J. (2013). Let Many Civil Societies Bloom: The Rise of Consultative
Authoritarianism in China. The China Quarterly, 213, 19-38.
doi:10.1017/S0305741012001269
Conventional wisdom suggests that an autonomous civil society cannot exist inside
authoritarian regimes and that the presence of civil society is an indicator of
democratization. In this article, the author challenges this view and shows that the
decentralization of public welfare and the linkage of bureaucratic promotion to the
delivery of these goods facilitated local government-civil society collaboration in China.
He calls this model "consultative authoritarianism," which encourages the simultaneous
expansion of a fairly autonomous civil society and the development of more indirect tools
of state control.
Counterviews:
• Levitsky, S., and L. Way. "The Myth of Democratic Recession". Journal of Democracy,
vol. 26, no. 1, Jan. 2015, pp. 45-58.
Levitsky and Way claim that there is no evidence of a global democratic recession and
the levels of global democracy have remained steady in the 2000s. The authors argue
that the misplaced warnings of a crisis of democracy are the result of undue optimism
about the spread of liberal democracy in the post-Cold War Era. It is this democratic
triumphalism that led scholars and analysts to equate authoritarian regime
weakening/liberalization in the 1990s with democratization. Hence, episodes of
authoritarian hardening are being widely misinterpreted as "democratic" backsliding in
regimes that are not even democratic to begin with. However, their argument does not
stand up to scrutiny in the face of mounting evidence of a persistent pattern of
backsliding in the last 15 or more years not just in new or weak electoral regimes but
also well-established democracies like the United States and India. Moreover, the
numbers of authoritarian regimes is also on the rise both absolute and relative to
democratic countries (see IDEA State of Democracy Report 2021)
• Foreign Affairs, The Dictator's Last Stand: Why the new Autocrats are Weaker than They
Look, 2019.
Argues that experts are overly pessimistic about the threats to democracy. Populist
leaders like Erdogan have an inherent legitimacy problem, as they concentrate power
their claims to represent "the people" become implausible. In addition, populist leaders
often lead to economic crises which can further weaken their rule. Although
acknowledging how some populist dictators can maintain power for the long-term, overall
argues that it is too early to say whether or not these regimes will survive.

about the US the proposals may have relevance for other democracies.

Europe to foreign malign influence. Also discussed Taiwan's efforts to counter

Halting Democratic Erosion/Building Resilience
Luca Tomini, Suzan Gibril & Venelin Bochev (2022), Standing up to autocratization: comparative
analysis of resistance actors and strategies, Democratization, 2022.
This article adds to the budding scholarship on countering autocratization by focusing on the
key actors resisting autocrats and their strategies across different types of regimes (full
democracy, electoral democracy-autocracy, autocracy). Using a comparative analysis of
selected cases of successful resistance, the authors identify three types of 'resisters' that exist
in different types of political systems. First, insider/institutional actors such as public officials and
judges in liberal democracies undergoing autocratization (e.g., the U.S. under Trump). Second,
16

political leaders/parties in electoral democracies/electoral autocracies acting through
parliamentary/democratic channels or extra-institutional mechanisms (e.g., Ecuador under
Correa). Finally, social/societal actors in full autocracies who resist autocrats via overt or covert
dissent, non-violent protests (e.g., Sudan since 2018).
Rising Hostility to Democracy Assistance: Can it be Countered? Carnegie Europe,
2022.
Democracy supporting organizations (DSOs) have sought to open up closed civic spaces in
hostile autocratizing regimes by supporting apolitical domestic actors, e.g., community forums,
theater groups, individual rights defenders & critical media (e.g., bloggers). But autocratic
regimes have tried to neutralize these actors, for example, through repressive legal, regulatory
and penal mechanisms. The authors suggest the need for the EU and other external donors to
get ahead of the curve by offering recommendations for a more directly political approach to
democracy assistance in hostile environments, such as developing mechanisms of discrete
support for social protest movements, and forging links between domestic and diaspora
activists.
Laebans & Luhrman, What Halts Democratic Erosion: The Role of Accountability,
Democratization, 2021.
This article focuses on the important role of accountability institutions to halt, if not prevent,
democratic erosion. The authors use the V-Dem Electoral Democracy Index to study three
recent success stories-Benin (2007-2012), Ecuador (2008-2010), and South Korea
(2008-2016). Their main finding is that three accountability mechanisms- parliamentary and
judicial oversight (horizontal accountability), pressures from civil society and the media (diagonal
accountability), and/or electoral competition between parties and within parties (vertical
accountability) - effectively stem erosion when they combine with institutional constraints-
such as presidential term limits or judicial independence - and contextual factors -such as
economic crises and public outrage about corruption scandals - to generate simultaneous
restraints on executive aggrandizement.
Anna Lührmann (2021) Disrupting the autocratization sequence: towards democratic resilience,
Democratization, 28:5, 1017-1039, DOI: 10.1080/13510347.2021.1928080
What can democratic actors do to disrupt autocratization in order to increase democratic
resilience? The author conceives autocratization as a three-stage sequence, arguing that each
of these stages provide opportunities for democratic actors to challenge would-be autocrats.
The first stage is the rise of public discontent with democratic institutions/parties, which can be
remedied by a better supply of democratic parties and processes as well as civic education. In
the second stage, autocratic/anti-democratic actors exploit and fuel public dissatisfaction to gain
17

power, which can be addressed through targeted sanctions against radicals and the mobilization
of moderate voters. Thirdly, once autocratization begins, strong accountability institutions and a
cohesive and creative opposition can help prevent democratic breakdown.
Murat Somer, Jennifer L. McCoy & Russell E. Luke (2021) Pernicious polarization,
autocratization and opposition strategies, Democratization, 28:5, 929-948, DOI:
10.1080/13510347.2020.1865316
The authors point to "pernicious polarization" - the elite-led division of society into mutually
distrustful Us versus Them camps -- as the driving force behind autocratization as it incentivizes
political actors to embrace democratically erosive actions. Using both theory and case studies,
they contend that the actions and objectives of democratic opposition are key to halting or
reversing such polarization. They offer a typology of opposition goals and strategies to analyze
the impact of polarization on democratic resilience.. Basically, oppositions face a choice
between generative or preservative goals on the one hand, and polarizing and depolarizing
strategies on the other. The gist: "active-depolarizing" & "transformative-repolarizing" strategies
are better than "passive-depolarizing" and "reciprocal polarizing" strategies, with the caveat that
that the tools (e.g., institutional accountability or voter mobilization) used to pursue these
choices/strategies will change as polarization deepens.
McCoy, J., & Somer, M. (2019). Toward a Theory of Pernicious Polarization and How It Harms
Democracies: Comparative Evidence and Possible Remedies. The ANNALS of the American
Academy of Political and Social Science, 681(1), 234-271.
[access or personal detail omitted]
This article (from a special issue of the Annals by the same authors) compares the dynamics of
polarization by drawing on case studies covered in the issue (e.g., Bangladesh, Turkey,
Hungary, Venezuela and the U.S.) to identify the causes, characteristics and mechanisms of
severe political polarization, and its consequences for democracy. Their key conclusion:
"pernicious polarization" (when a society is split into mutually distrustful "Us vs. Them camps) is
not attributable to any social, structural or institutional factors. Instead, it is a product of political
entrepreneurs advancing their political goals by using divisive narratives and exploiting existing
discontent/grievances, and the failure of their opponents to either adopt active depolarizing
strategies or their use of reactive polarizing tactics. They conclude with suggestions for
preventing polarization: judicial action against polarizing elites, the choices and strategies of
political and civil society opposition, such as effective electoral strategies, internal organizational
reforms, and support for democratic institutional reforms.
Vanessa A. Boese, Amanda B. Edgell, Sebastian Hellmeier, Seraphine F. Maerz & Staffan I.
Lindberg (2021) How democracies prevail: democratic resilience as a two-stage process,
Democratization, 28:5, 885-907, DOI: 10.1080/13510347.2021.1891413
18

This article unpacks democratic resilience as a two-stage process: autocratization onset and
democratic breakdown. Key finding: democracies have generally been resilient to the onset of
autocratization since 1900 but their resilience has eroded since the end of the Cold War. The
authors also find evidence that once autocratization starts, it can be difficult to stop: only one in
five democracies can manage to avert breakdown. Their analysis suggests that democratic
resilience is positively correlated with judicial constraints on the executive and past experience
with democracy. The article also contributes to modernization theory (democracy-development
linkage): higher levels of economic development are associated with resilience to the onset of
autocratization, but not to ongoing autocratization.
Cleary, M., & Öztürk, A. (2022). When Does Backsliding Lead to Breakdown? Uncertainty and
Opposition Strategies in Democracies at Risk. Perspectives on Politics, 20(1), 205-221.
doi: 10.1017/S1537592720003667
The authors explain why executive aggrandizement (or backsliding) leads to democratic
breakdown in some contexts but not in others. Drawing on case studies of Bolivia, Ecuador,

regime breakdown. Moderate opposition responses (using institutional mechanisms) work better

countries that remain non-democratic. Their evidence suggests that democracy induces
growth by increasing investments in public goods, improving the provision of schooling
and health care, and reducing social unrest.

qualitative analysis to argue that autocratic linkage increases regime survival.
• Tolstrup, Jakob. "Black Knights and Elections in Authoritarian Regimes: Why and How
Russia Supports Authoritarian Incumbents in post-Soviet States." European Journal of
Political Research 54 (2015): 673-690.
Develops 5 mechanisms through which autocratic regimes can support undemocratic
election outcomes in hybrid or authoritarian regimes: signaling invincibility through
campaign resources and help with electoral fraud, deterring elite defection from the
autocratic regime, undermining opposition activities, helping deal with popular protests,
and countervailing pro-democracy pressure from US/EU. Argues autocratic states are
most likely to interfere in elections when they fear that an opposition victory will lead to a
radical change threatening their strategic interests.
• Von Soest, Christian. "Democracy Prevention: The International Collaboration of
Authoritarian Regimes." European Journal of Political Research 54 (2015): 623-638.
Theorizes about how and why autocracy promotion occurs. Argues that authoritarian
states engage in authoritarian promotion for self-serving reasons, not ideology. They are
seeking to ensure their survival by supporting autocratic regimes, especially in regions
seen as geopolitically significant. Discusses the differences between authoritarian
diffusion, learning, collaboration, and support.
64

• Weyland, Kurt. "Autocratic Diffusion and Cooperation: The Impact of Interests vs.
Ideology." Democratization 24, no. 7 (2017): 1235-1252.
Discusses the different types of autocratic diffusion. One type is ideologically driven,
such as the Bolivarianism of Chavez. However, this is rare in the contemporary era
where most autocratic regimes lack ideological foundations and are instead driven by the
goal to prevent democratic diffusion and ensure their own regime's survival.
Critical Arguments (Think Autocratic Promotion Is Limited or Unproven):
• Brownlee, Jason. "The Limited Reach of Authoritarian Powers." Democratization 24, no.
7 (2017): 1326-1344.
Emphasizes the importance of local conditions, not external actors, to explain regime
outcomes, including democratic breakdown. Argues that potential autocracy promoters,
like Russia,maybe more concerned about which leaders are in power than whether a
regime is democratic or not. Brownlee argues that the evidence shows that authoritarian
states have acted to prevent democratization in their regions but are not globally
subverting democracy. [more recent data may challenge some of Brownlee's
conclusions as the erosion of democracy has continued since he conducted his research
4-5 years ago]
• Tansey, Oisin. "The Problem with Autocracy Promotion." Democratization 23, no. 1
(2016): 141-163.
Is generally critical of recent work on autocratic promotion and argues that current
research has not proven that autocracy promotion is a unified foreign policy approach
deliberately seeking to establish an autocratic state abroad. In other words, current
research has failed to prove the motives of states. Tansey offers a new, more narrowly
defined understanding of autocracy promotion that requires there be evidence that the
authoritarian promoter wants to support autocracy and has an ideological commitment to
autocracy.
• Way, Lucan. "The Limits of Autocracy Promotion: The Case of Russia in 'Near Abroad'."
European Journal of Political Research 54 (2015): 691-706.
Argues that Russia has been inconsistent in its support of authoritarianism in
neighboring states and that given the overall low level of democracy in those states that
we cannot prove Russia's actions have had a major impact. Overall, Way is skeptical
that autocratic promotion is a threat to democracy today.
Academic Theories about Authoritarianism
65

Background/Overview of Theorizing about How Authoritarian Regimes Work:
• Annals of Comparative Democratization. "What Do We Know About Contemporary
Autocracies and Autocratization?" January 2019.
Multiple relatively short articles written by prominent scholars that provide an overview of
the current academic research on autocracy/authoritarianism. Covers the topics of
democratic resilience, rise of more personalistic authoritarian regimes, the role of
elections in authoritarian regimes, and the importance of considering ideology.
• Cooley, Alexander. "Countering Democratic Norms." Journal of Democracy 26, no. 3
(July 2015): 49-63.
Discusses how authoritarian regimes, especially Russia, have used norms about state
security (especially counterterrorism), "civilizational diversity" (e.g., Western norms do
not apply here), and traditional values to counter the diffusion of democracy. Also
discusses the rise of GONGOs and pro-authoritarian regional organizations like ALBA.
• Gandhi, Jennifer and Ellen Lust-Okar. "Elections under Authoritarianism." Annual Review
of Political Science 12 (2009): 403-22.
A detailed discussion of the role of elections in dictatorships, including exploring the
specific mechanisms by how dictators use elections to stay in power and the
decision-making of voters, opposition leaders, and elites in relation to those elections.
One of the first major academic works that really explored this question.
• Geddes, Barbara, Joseph Wright, and Erica Frantz. How Dictatorships Work.
Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2018. (Book)
An influential, large-scale project by leading scholars that uses a systematic approach
based on analysis of 200 dictatorial regimes to theorize how dictators come to power,
how they govern, and how they lose power. Focuses on the importance of the initial
seizure group (political parties, military, or ruling family) for explaining the politics of
dictatorships. They conclude with several policy recommendations.
• Guriev, Sergei and Daniel Treisman. "Popularity of Authoritarian Leaders." World Politics
(2020).
• Lührmann, Anna, Juraj Medzihorsky, Staan I. Lindberg. "Walking the Talk: How to
Identify Anti-Pluralist Parties." V-Dem Working Paper, March 2021.
• Reuter, Ora John. "Why Do Ruling Parties Extend Authoritarian Rule? Examining the
Role of Elite Institutions and Mass Organization."V-Dem Working Paper, April 2021.
66

• Svolik, Milan W. "Power Sharing and Leadership Dynamics in Authoritarian Regimes."
American Journal of Political Science 53, no. 2 (2009): 477-494.
One of the important dynamics in an authoritarian regime is the relationship between the
dictator and ruling coalition--the individuals who support the government and hold
enough power along with the dictator to be sufficient to maintain power. Using a formal
modeling approach, Svolik argues that in authoritarian politics the nature of power
sharing between these two groups influences the longevity of the dictator and the
stability of the regime.
• Triesman, Daniel. "Democracy by Mistake: How the Errors of Autocrats Trigger
Transitions to Freer Government." American Political Science Review 114, no. 3 (August
2020): 792-810.
• Weidmann, Nils B. and Espen Geelmuyden Rød. The Internet and Political Protest in
Autocracies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2019. (Book)
Weidmann and Rod take a nuanced approach to how the internet is influencing protests
in autocracies. They find that digital repression helps keep the levels of protests low, but
once a protest movement starts Internet technology can intensify and help spread the
unrest to other cities, especially if there are higher levels of connectivity. They developed
a new database of mass mobilization in autocracies and used that to engage in
statistical analysis of protests in 60 autocracies at the city level.
Recent publications:
• Kavasoglu, Berker. "Opposition Parties and Elite Co-optation in Electoral Autocracies."
V-Dem Working Paper (2021).
• Kreko, Peter. "How Authoritarians Inflate Their Image." Journal of Democracy 32, no. 3
(July 2021): 109-123.
Kreko argues that authoritarian powers, especially Russia, are inflating their image on
the global stage to look more economically, politically, and militarily powerful than they
actually are, and therefore exaggerating their power and influence. Focusing on Europe,
argues that the images of Russia & China have become distorted because of the
combination of disinformation campaigns, investments for political purposes, receptive
national politicians (e.g., Orban in Hungary), and the diminished attraction of the
Western democratic economic liberal model.
• Melendez-Sanchez, Manuel. "Latin America Erupts: Millennial Authoritarianism in El
Salvador." Journal of Democracy 32, no. 3 (July 2021): 19-32.
67

Argues that Nayib Bukele managed to rise to power in El Salvador because of "millennial
authoritarianism," a "political strategy that combines traditional populist appeals, classic
authoritarian behavior, and a youthful and modern brand built primarily via social media."
"Democratic Regressions in Asia," Special Issue, Democratization, 2021.
Special issue of the journal Democratization focusing on democratic decline and revival
in the Asia-Pacific region, divided into two sections: thematic and case studies. Articles
include an introduction covering the state of the research and patterns of democratic
regression in the region, the scope and causes of democratic backsliding in comparative
perspective (by the prominent American democracy scholar, Larry Diamond), the causes
and mechanisms of democratic regressions, deconsolidation in Japan, Korea and
Taiwan; civil society resistance to autocratization in Indonesia; pathways of backsliding in
Bangladesh; the role of local election monitors in democratic revival across the region;
elite capture and civil society (Bangladesh, Philippines and Thailand); China's autocratic
influence on Hong Kong as well as backsliding in regional governance
mechanisms/ASEAN and foriegn policy in Southeast Asia.
Academic Theories on Democratic Decline
• Maerz, Seraphine F., Carsten Q. Schneider. "Public Discourse and Autocratization:
Infringing on Autonomy, Sabotaging Accountability." V-Dem Working Paper, February
2021.
• Lührmann, Anna, and Bryan Rooney. "Autocratization by Decree: States of Emergency
and Democratic Decline." V-Dem Working Paper, April 2020.
